Today, we laid out our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive, end-to-end software delivery system in the world.

Our jobs as developers are changing. In a couple of years, we’ve gone from writing every line of code to working with AI assistants to orchestrating fleets of agents. But the goal hasn’t changed: ship completed software work. A feature, a bug fix, a security fix. Completed work, not more code, is the output that matters.

Today at GitHub Universe, we shared our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive software delivery system in the world. We introduced products that bring that vision to life and showed how we’re rebuilding the infrastructure underneath it.

The SDLC is no longer a linear path from planning to coding to testing to deployment. A code change, a request from a colleague, or a production metric can trigger work anywhere in the system. Most of us (and our agents) jump between different stages, depending on the task at hand. Developers set the direction, make decisions, and stay accountable for what ships. Agents implement and verify changes. And everything feeds into and out of a continuous learning machine that makes the next cycle better.

This agentic software delivery system solves for three things:

GitHub is built for developers and their agents. We’re also making the underlying primitives available, so you can build your own bespoke solutions. You stay in control of the work, the tools, and the cost.

Today at Universe, we showed some of the latest products and features in action, starting with the GitHub Copilot app.

The GitHub Copilot app is designed from the ground up for agentic software delivery. It connects your agents and tools across projects, so you can direct the work without making every handoff. And it’s for more than producing code: you can write specs, present design discussions, or analyze telemetry in one agent-first surface.

Different tasks need different models. Developers shouldn’t have to manage every model choice to get the right result at the right price. Copilot Fusion evaluates what a task needs across reasoning, code generation, debugging, and tool use, then chooses how to execute across one or more models. In the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Fusion Max scored within two points of Opus 5.5 Max at half the cost and 40% less time per task.

Available natively in the GitHub Copilot app starting today, Copilot projects let you run agent work across multiple repos in fully managed, parallel sessions. You have one place to track progress, make decisions, and direct what happens next. That means you can spend less time managing execution and more time deciding what’s worth building.

Your work shouldn’t restart when you switch devices or tools. Session continuity lets you start and follow the same cloud agent session across the GitHub app, VS Code, the CLI, and the web. Start from your phone at standup, steer it from VS Code at your desk, and check in on it from github.com at lunch. The agent keeps working in the cloud. Our multi-model harness that enables it is powerful, fast, and cost-efficient.

Copilot automations let you create AI-powered workflows within your repo. They run in the cloud, and you can kick them off manually or set them up to respond to an event or run on a schedule. That lets you coordinate agents to handle tasks such as issue triage and code review. And now, automations can learn from their outcomes and propose improvements for you to review and approve. That’s the learning engine in practice. Use the results of the completed work to make the next run better.

More code means more pull requests and more demand for review. Moving faster only helps if we can maintain the quality of what ships. Copilot code review surfaces meaningful, actionable bugs that developers need to catch. Today, we introduced Copilot code review Max, which posted the highest F1 score on ReviewBench for high-severity issues. Lite and Balanced keep everyday reviews fast; the new Max provides a deeper look when a change needs it.

Starting today, GitHub Enterprise customers can use all Copilot features without buying a separate subscription. That includes GitHub Copilot app, code review, automations, and more. You pay for the AI credits you use.

This is available through GitHub Sales today, with self-serve coming soon. Existing Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise customers can keep their current plans or move over when they’re ready. GitHub also remains open and extensible. Keep using the tools your team depends on, including Cloudflare, Datadog, Figma, and more.

All of this depends on a foundation that’s fast, reliable, and built to scale. Agents are changing the volume and shape of software development. Adding capacity matters, but capacity alone won’t get us there. We’ve also had to change the architecture.

We’re also migrating to a multi-region deployment in Azure, while continuing to serve incredible levels of traffic from developers around the world. We expect to complete the migration early next year. Those investments give us more room to grow. The next step is building the systems that handle the work.

We’ve scaled Git for years as activity on GitHub has grown. The agentic era calls for a different ceiling on throughput and reliability. Three principles guide our new Git architecture: simplify the primitives, decouple storage from compute, and minimize coordination.

Git’s just one example of the work we’re doing to scale the platform. We’ve done a lot of work across GitHub’s AI gateway, the harness, and much more.

Our jobs are changing, but developers are more important than ever. I think all the software we’ve written to date will amount to less than 1% of the software we’ll write in the next five years. The opportunity isn’t just to produce more code. It’s to solve problems we couldn’t solve before.

That’s why we’re connecting the full software delivery system, giving developers better ways to work with agents, and evolving the infrastructure for what comes next. And we’re doing it on GitHub, where we can build together.

Jay Parikh is a seasoned executive, board member, and advisor to some of the world’s fastest growing and most successful consumer, developer, and enterprise technology companies. As Executive Vice President of CoreAI at Microsoft, Parikh leads the organization building the end-to-end agentic system required to build, ship, and run AI agents in the Enterprise. His teams, including GitHub, also build the tools and platforms developers need to create the next generation of software.

Previously, Parikh was CEO of a cloud security startup and, before that, was Facebook’s global head of engineering and infrastructure. For more than a decade, he led the teams that built and operated the physical infrastructure and software that supported the company’s growth from 300 million people to more than 3 billion. His teams worked across the stack, from data centers, servers, and subsea cables to software, data, AI, and security systems. Through leadership roles in the Open Compute Project and Telecom Infra Project, he helped extend infrastructure innovation beyond a single company to benefit entire industries.

Earlier in his career, Parikh held leadership roles at Akamai and Ning. He brings a systems thinker’s perspective to a deeply human challenge: how to build teams that keep learning, moving, and delivering as the world changes around them.

Writing code got faster. The work around it didn’t. See how you can plan, write code, review changes, and investigate production issues with GitHub Copilot, and what work still needs your judgment.

#10029. Shipping huggingface_hub every week with AI, open tools, and a human in the loop

huggingface_hub is the Python client at the base of the Hugging Face ecosystem. transformers, datasets, diffusers, sentence-transformers and dozens of other libraries depend on it to talk to the Hub. Every week we don't ship a new release is a week of fixes and features stuck on main.

For a long time we released every 4 to 6 weeks. We now release every week from a single GitHub Actions workflow. We built it using open-source tools and open-weights models and kept a human in the loop at the one place where judgment matters. Nothing in this post requires a vendor contract, a closed model, or infrastructure you can't run yourself. That was a design goal from the start since we wanted a workflow other maintainers could pick up and adapt.

By the end of this post, you'll have everything you need to build your own.

The old process was partly automated, mostly manual.

Writing good notes for a new version was the heavy part, aggregating tens of PRs on different topics. Nothing technically hard but a few hours of focused attention. Add the announcements on top and a minor release was easily a half-day of work spread over several days.

So we decided to streamline the whole thing. Looking at that list, the work splits in two.

Some steps are purely mechanical and can be automated: bumping the version, committing, tagging, pushing, opening downstream test branches, opening the post-release PR. Nobody needs to think about those. They just have to happen in the right order, every time, which is what a CI workflow is good at.

The rest is different. Writing release notes, deciding what to highlight, phrasing an announcement for a human audience: that's brain work. It's the kind of judgment that kept the release manual for years. This is where AI comes in, turning a blank page into a solid first draft in seconds. It's also where we have to be careful because a draft that looks confident and is subtly wrong is worse than no draft at all.

When we decided to fix this, we set one constraint up front: every moving part had to be something any maintainer could run themselves. No closed model behind an API we couldn't swap, no proprietary release platform, no secret sauce.

The second principle: the model drafts, a human decides. Language models are good at turning thirty terse PR titles into readable release notes. They are not good at being trusted blindly. So the workflow is human-supervised: the model does the first pass, a deterministic script checks its work, and a human reviews and edits before anything ships (more on that below).

The full workflow is a single file, .github/workflows/release.yml, triggered by hand from the Actions UI. It takes exactly one input:

From there, the jobs run roughly in this order:

The remaining manual steps are reviewing and publishing the draft release notes, and reviewing and posting an internal Slack message. Those two steps are where we want a human in the loop.

Here's the failure mode everyone worries about with AI-generated release notes: the model quietly drops a PR or invents one that isn't in this release. A changelog that's almost right is worse than no changelog because nobody re-checks it.

We don't trust the generated release notes to be complete on the first try, we verify it deterministically. Before the model runs, a Python script retrieves all PRs that belong to the release and stores them as ground truth.

Then model drafts the notes from them. Once done, we check its output against the initial list of PRs:

If anything is missing or extra, we don't fail and we don't ship a wrong file. We hand the discrepancy back to the agent and ask it to fix exactly those PRs:

This is the pattern that makes the whole thing trustworthy: a non-deterministic model wrapped in deterministic guardrails. The model is great at writing prose and unreliable at being exhaustive. So we let it write and let code enforce the consistency.

Completeness is one half. Accuracy is the other. A model summarizing a PR from its title alone will cheerfully invent a code example that doesn't match the real API.

To prevent that, when we fetch PR metadata we also pull the actual documentation diffs from each PR: the unified diff of any .md file under docs/ that the PR touched.

That diff goes into the model's context so when it writes "here's the new CLI command," it's quoting the example the PR author actually wrote in the docs. That's the same logic as before: give the model real source material and a narrow job.

The prompts themselves live as Skills: small Markdown files (SKILL.md plus reference templates) checked into the repo. The release-notes skill spells out how to pick highlights, how to structure sections, when to add a doc link, etc. It reads like onboarding instructions, which is exactly the right mental model.

After the RC is published, the draft GitHub release sits there with the AI's first pass in it. This is where the human comes in:

The reviewer's time goes into polishing, turning a half-day of writing into a fifteen-minute editing session.

We also keep a paper trail to improve over time. We archive two files side by side to a Hugging Face Bucket: the raw AI draft, uploaded at RC time before anyone touches it, and the human-edited version, uploaded when the final release is cut.

Collecting both every week gives us a growing dataset of "what the model wrote" versus "what we wished it wrote". Dataset that we can then reuse to update the agent's skill.

Revamping the release process was a good opportunity to tighten security, especially against supply-chain attacks.

No PyPI token. Publishing uses Trusted Publishing: PyPI verifies a short-lived OIDC token minted by GitHub for this exact workflow, and issues PEP 740 attestations / Sigstore provenance for every artifact. There's no long-lived secret to leak or rotate.

The agent runtime is pinned and verified. We don't curl | bash the latest OpenCode and hope. We pin a version and check its SHA256 before running it:

Open tooling doesn't mean careless tooling.

Almost nothing. A full release (notes plus the Slack announcement, across 20-40 PRs and a few rounds of prompting) costs about $0.25 on Inference Providers. With open weights billed pay-as-you-go, the only real question each week is "is there something worth shipping?", and there always is.

The cadence went from one release every 4 to 6 weeks to once a week. The secondary effects were the interesting ones:

This is the part we cared about most. The workflow is shaped around huggingface_hub but the structure is generic.

To adapt it: fork the workflow file and scripts, point it at your package, rewrite the skill Markdown for your project's voice, set two repo variables (the model ID and your OpenCode version), set up Trusted Publishing on PyPI, and delete the downstream-testing job if you don't have downstreams. The trust-but-verify loop is the part worth reusing as-is. It's what makes a generated artifact safe to ship.

The parts of a release that used to need a half-day of focused human work (writing notes, drafting announcements, coordinating downstream checks) are the parts a model is good at drafting. Everything else is mechanical and fits in a YAML file. The trick was never just "let the AI do it". It's to let the model draft, let deterministic code verify, and let a human decide. It's built entirely from open tools and open weights so the cost rounds to zero and anyone can run it.

The full workflow file is public. If you maintain a Python library, fork it, adapt it, and let us know how it goes!

Thanks for the post! This will help so many people 🤗

GitHub’s annual month-long game jam is back for its 14th year! This November, make a game inspired by the theme SHIFT. Change gears, swap perspectives, bend reality, or just press a certain key.

Game Off, GitHub’s annual month-long game jam, returns for its 14th year this November. Thousands of developers have joined us over the years to make everything from polished platformers to wonderfully weird experiments.

Whether you’re making your first game or your fiftieth, we’d love for you to join us.

Shift gears. Shift perspectives. Shift dimensions. Shift bits. Work the night shift. Or make a game where the only buttons are the Shift keys.

How you interpret the theme is entirely up to you.

You have until December 1, 2026, at 13:37 PST to build and submit a game inspired by SHIFT. Strong or loose inspirations apply!

Acronyms (that we definitely just made up)

Or invent your own. We love seeing where you take the theme.

Of course, you could also build a game about shifting tectonic plates, shape-shifting aliens, shifting alliances, shifting sands, or a particularly ambitious stick shift.

Don’t overthink it. Pick an interpretation that interests you and see where it takes you.

Pro tip: Start with one mechanic and one playable level. Get those working before adding the multiverse. Future you (and your bug tracker) will thank you.

Need another perspective? Try brainstorming with GitHub Copilot. Give it the theme, a few constraints, and see what it comes up with:

Work alone or form a team. Use whichever programming languages, game engines, frameworks, libraries, and tools make sense for your game.

Here’s the fun part: you decide who wins.

Once submissions close, it’s your turn to play and rate the games your fellow developers have created. Every vote helps determine which games take home the bragging rights.

Entries will be evaluated in the following categories:

Voting will end on January 1, 2027, at 13:37 PST. Winners will be announced on the GitHub Blog and GitHub social channels shortly thereafter.

Game Off is intentionally relaxed, but there are a few guidelines to help keep it fair and fun:

That’s it. Keep it creative, respectful, and fun… and make sure your final code is pushed before the deadline.

You don’t need to be an expert to participate. Many Game Off participants create their first game during the jam.

Some use established engines. Some build their own. Others make games for old consoles, unusual hardware, terminals, calculators, or platforms we assumed had been lost to time.

However you build your game, there’s no single correct way to play.

Here are a few engines and frameworks you might want to explore:

Looking for teammates or a place to share progress? The Game Off 2026 Community is a great place to ask questions, share progress, and look for teammates. There’s also a friendly community-run Discord server.

Game Off is the perfect opportunity to check it out. Version control pun fully intended.

Whether you spend November shifting pixels, shifting bits, shifting timelines, or shifting unfinished tasks into the final 24 hours, you’ll be part of a global community making games together.

So take a different perspective, change the rules, and see what happens when you press ⇧.

Good luck and have fun! Can’t wait to play, err, test all your games! <3

Senior Program Manager, GitHub Developer Relations. Open source hype man, AI whisperer, hackathon and game jam wrangler. I write && manage programs, support dev communities, and occasionally ship something.

#10027. Introducing the FFASR Leaderboard: Benchmarking ASR in the Real World

🚀 First open far-field ASR benchmark: community-driven evaluation across 14 simulated rooms, validated against real-world measurements: https://huggingface.co/spaces/treble-technologies/ffasr

📉 The gap is real and it is large: across all submitted models, far-field WER at low SNR is consistently several times higher than near-field WER on the same speech content

🔬 Methodology you can trust: hybrid wave-based simulation, sim-to-real validation, moving-source splits in beta, held-out audio, and standardized evaluation hardware across all submissions

⚡ Accuracy and speed together: the Pareto front plots average WER against RTFx so you can evaluate the tradeoff that is right for your deployment

👀 More is coming: multi-talker scenarios, microphone array support, and echo cancellation are on the roadmap

The gap between benchmark performance and real-world deployment is one of the more persistent frustrations in ASR development. Models that score well on standard evaluations often behave differently once real room acoustics are involved: reverberation, background noise, microphone distance. The complex interactions between these factors affect performance in ways that clean-speech benchmarks do not capture. The FFASR Leaderboard is our attempt to quantify that gap.

Treble Technologies and Hugging Face are launching the Far-Field ASR (FFASR) Leaderboard, the first open, community-driven benchmark designed to evaluate ASR models under realistic far-field acoustic conditions. It is live now, and we are inviting the community to submit models, explore the results, and help shape what comes next.

Voice interfaces have expanded well beyond the headset and the smartphone. AI voice agents, conference room transcription, in-car assistants, humanoid robots, smart glasses, and hands-free tools are all seeing rapid adoption. What they have in common is that they operate in acoustically complex environments: reverberation, background noise, overlapping sounds, and a microphone that may be anywhere from one to several meters from the speaker.

The dominant ASR evaluation paradigm has not caught up with this reality. Clean, close-microphone benchmarks remain the standard, and while they are useful for measuring core recognition quality, they do not predict far-field performance. A model that performs well on LibriSpeech or other near-field sets may degrade substantially once real room acoustics enter the picture. While there have been several research efforts around far-field and noisy speech evaluation — including CHiME, URGENT, and NOIZEUS — the community has not had a standardized, open way to measure that degradation consistently across models in a continuously updated leaderboard format. That is what FFASR is built for.

A major challenge of far-field evaluation is the availability of data. Collecting far-field recordings across a representative range of room types, microphone distances, and noise conditions at scale is prohibitively expensive with physical measurements alone. Simulation makes it possible to cover that space systematically and to extend coverage over time without a corresponding increase in measurement cost.

Another goal of FFASR is to encourage the development of models that are explicitly robust to these conditions. Leaderboards have historically been effective at directing research effort. By making far-field performance visible and comparable, we hope to raise the priority of real-world acoustic robustness across the field.

The FFASR Leaderboard evaluates models across nine conditions. The four that determine the primary ranking score are (as of 22 June 2026):

To give a sense of what these conditions actually sound like, the samples below let you hear the same speech utterance as dry anechoic audio, then convolved with a room impulse response, and finally with noise added at each SNR tier. The difference between the dry recording and the low-SNR far-field condition is a reasonable proxy for the scale of the problem the leaderboard is measuring.

Two additional columns, Lab Measured and Lab Simulated, serve as a sim-to-real validation track. The leaderboard also includes moving-source splits, currently in beta, which evaluate models against audio where the speaker is in motion rather than stationary. This condition reflects use cases such as humanoid robots, in-car speech, and mobile voice assistants where the acoustic geometry between speaker and microphone changes continuously.

The acoustic data is generated with Treble's hybrid simulation engine, which combines a wave-based solver at low to mid frequencies with geometrical-acoustics modeling at higher frequencies. This approach captures physical phenomena that simpler simulation methods often miss: diffraction, scattering, interference, and modal behavior. The result is simulated data that closely matches measured acoustic conditions, which the Lab Measured and Lab Simulated columns confirm directly by running the same evaluation on both.

Fourteen fully furnished rooms are included in the benchmark, ranging from 20 to 470 m³ and covering bathrooms, living rooms with hallways, offices, classrooms, and restaurant spaces. Each acoustic scene contains one target speaker, recorded in an anechoic chamber to avoid reverberation artifacts from the recording environment, and up to three noise sources. Every scene includes both a transient noise source such as coughing and a continuous noise source such as HVAC, at three SNR levels. This coverage is designed to reflect the actual variety of spaces where deployed voice systems operate.

Alongside WER, the leaderboard reports RTFx (audio seconds per inference second) for every submission, evaluated on an NVIDIA L4 GPU under identical conditions. Accuracy and latency together are what matter in real deployments, and the Pareto front view in the Analysis tab makes that tradeoff explicit.

This benchmark is build on simulated acoustic spaces via Treble Technologies proprietaty simulation engine. An example of the output from the enginge can be found in the Treble10 dataset released last year, which established the simulation pipeline and made far-field RIRs available for training and research. FFASR extends that foundation into a standardized evaluation framework with a held-out test set, consistent normalization, and automated scoring.

With the leaderboard live, a consistent pattern is emerging across all submitted models: the gap between near-field and far-field performance is large, and it grows significantly as SNR decreases. Near-field WER values, on clean dry speech, look comparable to what the same models achieve on established benchmarks. Far-field WER at low SNR tells a different story, often several times higher. The benchmark makes this degradation visible and comparable in a way that was previously difficult to do outside proprietary evaluation pipelines.

The Pareto front of average WER against RTFx is also revealing. There is a genuine spectrum of approaches represented in the current submissions: models that prioritize speed at the cost of some accuracy, models that push accuracy at the cost of throughput, and a smaller number that achieve a competitive position on both axes. Visualizing these tradeoffs against far-field accuracy rather than clean-speech accuracy produces a materially different picture of where the real differences between systems lie. The Analysis tab is worth exploring beyond the main ranking table.

One observation worth highlighting for developers: the leaderboard reports both near-field (dry) and far-field WER side by side. This separation is intentional and useful. It makes it possible to distinguish between a model that is genuinely accurate and one that is accurate but brittle to acoustic conditions, which matters for deciding whether to invest in far-field fine-tuning, speech enhancement preprocessing, or a different architecture altogether.

Open the Submit tab on the FFASR Leaderboard, paste a Hugging Face model ID, and evaluation runs server-side against the held-out dataset. The pipeline supports Whisper variants, IBM Granite Speech, Cohere Transcribe, Wav2Vec2 and HuBERT CTC heads, SpeechBrain ASR, and most other ASR architectures on the Hub without any custom configuration.

For teams using more complex inference stacks, including systems that combine speech enhancement with ASR, a custom evaluator option allows you to define your own evaluate() function. Custom evaluators run on Hub Jobs after moderator review, and the submission notes field is a good place to document any preprocessing steps so results are interpretable by others.

The held-out evaluation set uses 2,000 anechoic speech samples across 14 rooms at three SNR tiers, approximately 8 hours of audio per condition, with Whisper-style text normalization applied consistently. The audio is not exposed to submitters, to avoid test-set contamination.

The conditions we are actively exploring for future tracks include multi-talker scenarios, where more than one speaker is active simultaneously, microphone array evaluation, covering beamforming and spatial filtering approaches, and echo cancellation, relevant for any device that plays audio while also listening.

What we build next will depend on where the community tells us the gaps are largest. If you work on a deployment environment or a use case that is not well represented in the current benchmark, we want to hear from you. The FFASR Leaderboard is designed to grow, and the direction it grows should reflect real needs.

Submit your model, explore the Analysis tab, post your ideas and suggestions on the FFASR forum, and help us build a benchmark that is actually useful for the problems the field is working on.

Far-Field ASR — clean / noisy / reverberant benchmark

Btw one related idea I've had sitting on the back of my mind: there's a class of synthetic audio scenarios that don't really occur naturally but are both tricky and relevant to real deployments.

Most ASR models lately seem geared toward clean meeting transcription. But if you run a Granola style setup that pulls every audio stream on your machine and mixes them together, things get messy fast. The system audio from the meeting, your physical hardware mic, and sometimes your own voice echoing back through the meeting can all be mixed/delayed/noisy in the same track the model sees. (I use VibeVoice for this myself since I figured it would be more robust; it's held up okay, but I haven't done a real comparison)

Mixed multi-stream audio like that feels like a natural fit for the kind of robustness/"real world scenario" this benchmark is measuring, even though it's a synthetic condition rather than a recorded room

Far-Field ASR — clean / noisy / reverberant benchmark

Louis Erbkamm built the first prototype in his free time. Now GitHub Copilot helps him maintain it alone.

Louis Erbkamm knows his way around Arnis, the smallest town in Germany, but he’s never set foot in it.

I know where the shops are. Where the boats are… I know the city pretty well, but I haven’t been there yet.

Arnis is also the name of his open source project, which takes real-world data from OpenStreetMap and other sources to turn places you know into Minecraft worlds you can freely explore. Since Louis started Arnis in 2022, it’s reached close to 900,000 downloads from GitHub and about 70 contributors.

Louis grew up playing Minecraft and started coding at 13, always looking for ways to bring code into the game. Arnis began as a fun diversion combining Minecraft with geospatial data, and it went on GitHub, where he already kept his side projects. He finished the first prototype within two weeks while on a break from school.

That first version was Python written by hand, built only on OpenStreetMap, and generating a town took a while. He needed somewhere real to test it, so he looked up towns in Germany, where he lives, and found Arnis. A small town helped while early generation was slow.

Arnis has a lot of buildings, it has streets, it has waters, it has all kinds of different elements that are useful to test with.

The project didn’t have a name yet, so it borrowed the town’s unique moniker.

When Arnis added elevation, its worlds stopped being flat, and geospatial specialists from all over showed up with ideas on how best to integrate it. They started discussions on their own, and Louis says that’s exactly what he needed.

Bigger calls happen in the open too: before porting Arnis from Python to Rust, Louis opened discussions on GitHub to hear different perspectives. Contributors have since translated Arnis into about 20 languages and built major features of their own.

The best thing that has happened to me is essentially this big community on GitHub to see actually people from all kinds of different fields coming together to work on something that I started as a side project.

Some features start on a walk. Louis noticed how many trash bins there were in his city, and there were none in his generated worlds.

Minecraft has no dedicated bins, so he took the question to the community, and together they found a block that fit. Placing one follows the same path as everything else: for the area a user selects, Arnis queries OpenStreetMap for every mapped element, then looks up each element’s coordinates and type.

If an element isn’t mapped, Arnis can’t place it. For structures too detailed for the map to describe, like the Statue of Liberty in New York, or Christ the Redeemer in Rio de Janeiro, Arnis converts 3D models into Minecraft blocks.

As the sole maintainer, Louis reviews every pull request himself, and they stack up. He usually spends evenings or weekends working on Arnis, which means the community has to wait for him to be done with work for the day.

He uses GitHub Copilot to get an overview of open issues and bugs from the latest release, see how many people are running into them, trace where a bug came from in the codebase, and create a fix. Since he brought AI into the project, he says, code reviews and documentation have both increased.

I could delegate those annoying and boring tasks to Copilot, while I could still have a look at those really cool topics that are related to the development of it.

Big features arrive as big pull requests.

Louis opens a large pull request in the GitHub Copilot app for a first overview and a performance review, with Copilot running in the background looking for small changes that would cut memory usage or generation time.

It takes just one wrong calculation in street lights, for example, to make the generation time of an entire city much slower.

He also keeps a mental list of the areas of the codebase that need extra care whenever someone changes them, and he has written the same warnings out by hand over and over.

I’m starting a few sub agents with the GitHub Copilot app to have a look specifically at those cases, and to come up with corner cases to test to make sure that we do not introduce any regressions into new releases.

He likes that the terminal, his files, the code changes and the pull request all sit in one app next to the chat.

Louis’s favorite use of Arnis is in schools, where teachers have generated their city or a neighborhood park.

Some turn it into a contest: every student starts from the same generated area, improves a nearby park or playground using Arnis and Minecraft, and the class looks at the results together.

Recent releases have gone beyond the bounds of Earth, adding the Moon and Mars. Louis wants Arnis to stay easy to use while getting closer to reality, with more detail in less time, and he would like to see it in more schools.

Download Arnis from github.com/louis-e/arnis, pick a place on the map, choose where to spawn, and click Start Generation: within a few minutes, the world is ready to open in Minecraft. Louis suggests a place you know, like your hometown or somewhere memorable you’ve been, such as the Grand Canyon or Niagara Falls. Then look for what’s missing.

So maybe you see a bench that was not generated even though it is there.

Map it on OpenStreetMap, or tell Louis if it’s a bug and he will fix it.

Writing code got faster. The work around it didn’t. See how you can plan, write code, review changes, and investigate production issues with GitHub Copilot, and what work still needs your judgment.

#10025. Accelerating Transformers Fine-Tuning with NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel

HuggingFace Transformers has become the foundation of the open-source AI ecosystem, and the recent Transformers v5 release strengthened it with first-class support for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, now the dominant architecture for frontier models. v5 ships the MoE foundations: expert backends, dynamic weight loading, and distributed execution that make MoE extensible and easy to build on.

NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel is an open library part of the NVIDIA NeMo framework for building custom generative AI models at scale. NeMo AutoModel builds cleanly on top of v5, adding Expert Parallelism, DeepEP fused all-to-all dispatch, and TransformerEngine kernels, and it leans on v5's dynamic weight loading to bring those optimizations to a broad and growing set of model families. The payoff is 3.4-3.7x higher training throughput and 29-32% less GPU memory on fine-tuning MoE models than native Transformers v5, using the same from_pretrained() API: a single import line, with no other code changes.

This blog details how this combination works and how users can fine-tune MoE models faster without changing their APIs.

The rise of MoE models has introduced new challenges to efficient training: Routing tokens across hundreds of experts, fusing expert matmuls into a single kernel, sharding weights across GPUs, and overlapping communication with computation all require infrastructure beyond what a general-purpose library provides out of the box.

Transformers v5 (“v5”) introduced first-class MoE support such as expert backends, dynamic weight loading, and tensor parallel plans for distributed execution. In addition, v5 made distributed training first-class by integrating PyTorch's DeviceMesh directly into from_pretrained().

NeMo AutoModel builds on top of v5 by subclassing AutoModelForCausalLM, and adding Expert Parallelism (EP), DeepEP fused all-to-all dispatch, and TransformerEngine kernels. DeepEP is the piece v5 doesn't have yet: it overlaps communication with expert compute. And because NeMo AutoModel rides v5's reversible weight conversion to load each model, it can focus its engineering on these reusable core ops instead of per-model checkpoint plumbing, while save_pretrained() still emits standard HF checkpoints that tools like vLLM and SGLang can load.

The next section walks through how the two work together and the performance gains we measured, from full fine-tuning NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B A55B across 16 nodes down to single-node models such as Qwen3-30B-A3B and Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B.

One of NeMo AutoModel's goals is API compatibility with HuggingFace Transformers to enable open-source community. NeMoAutoModelForCausalLM subclasses AutoModelForCausalLM, so any code that works with HF models works with AutoModel too.

Here's what loading a model looks like in both. Only the import changes:

That single import does a lot of work. For popular MoE architectures like Qwen3, NVIDIA Nemotron, GPT-OSS, and DeepSeek V3, NeMo AutoModel ships hand-tuned implementations with TransformerEngine attention, fused linear layers, and custom expert kernels. For everything else, it falls back to vanilla HF while still applying optimizations like Liger kernel patching, among others. And whichever path it takes, the resulting model is ready to scale: pass a device_mesh and you have multi-GPU training without further rewrites.

Where NeMo AutoModel really shines is scaling MoE models to multi-GPU training. To train Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B with Expert Parallelism across 8 GPUs, one adds the distributed mesh configuration:

This gives speed, scalability and memory-optimizations with FSDP2, Expert Parallelism, TransformerEngine kernels and DeepEP dispatch, all from a from_pretrained() call.

We evaluated NeMo AutoModel in two regimes: full fine-tuning a frontier-scale 550B model across 16 nodes, and training two 30B MoE models on a single node. The 550B result shows why Expert Parallelism is essential at scale; the 30B results quantify the per-GPU speedup over Transformers v5.

Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B A55B is a 550B-parameter hybrid model shipping with Mamba2, LatentMoE, and Multi-Token Prediction (MTP). We benchmark a full fine-tune: every parameter is updated and the Adam optimizer state is materialized, which at this scale spans 16 H100 nodes (128 GPUs).

Why there is no Transformers v5 column. Transformers v5 runs out of memory at this scale, so there is no v5 number to report here. AutoModel's Expert Parallelism shards the experts across GPUs to bring the footprint within budget, which is what lets the full fine-tune run. The 30B comparisons below show the same advantage where v5 fits.

We benchmarked three approaches on a single node with 8x H100 80GB GPUs: HF Transformers v4 (hub code), HF Transformers v5 (with best available optimizations), and NeMo AutoModel (EP=8 + custom kernels).

A note on the routing gate. The NeMo AutoModel numbers below use a balanced routing gate, which forces tokens to be distributed uniformly across experts. This emulates the ideal operating point an MoE is trained toward: a well-trained model's load-balancing loss drives expert utilization to near-uniform, so balanced routing reflects the steady-state a real workload converges to (and removes the straggler noise that random dummy tokens otherwise inject into expert parallelism). v4/v5 run their native router on the same dummy tokens. The balanced gate therefore measures NeMo AutoModel at its target MoE operating point, and the v4/v5 columns reflect their out-of-the-box behavior.

Why v4 deadlocks: Transformers v4 stores Qwen3 MoE experts as a ModuleList of 128 individual MLP modules, each separately FSDP-wrapped. The forward pass uses a data-dependent loop that only iterates experts that received tokens. With different data per rank, different ranks skip different experts, causing mismatched FSDP AllGather/ReduceScatter collectives and an indefinite hang. Transformers v5 fixes this by storing experts as fused 3D parameter tensors (no per-expert modules, no per-expert FSDP collectives).

v4 config: trust_remote_code=True (NVIDIA's hub modeling code). The hub code's expert loop is FSDP-safe (iterates all experts regardless of token assignment), so it doesn't deadlock like Qwen3 v4.

The 3.4-3.7x speedup from NeMo AutoModel over Transformers v5 comes from three sources:

Expert Parallelism reduces memory pressure. EP=8 distributes expert weights across GPUs, cutting the per-GPU MoE footprint by 8x. For Qwen3, this drops peak memory from 68.2 GiB to 48.1 GiB (-29%). For Nemotron Nano, it drops from 62.1 GiB to 42.5 GiB (-32%), freeing headroom for larger batch sizes or longer sequences.

DeepEP fuses communication with computation. Instead of separate AllGather/ReduceScatter collectives for expert routing, DeepEP fuses token dispatch and combines into optimized GPU kernels, overlapping communication with expert computation.

TransformerEngine kernels accelerate core operations. TE's fused attention, linear layers, and RMSNorm implementations provide consistent speedups over their PyTorch/Flash Attention equivalents across all layer types, not just MoE layers.

One of the most impactful features in Transformers v5 is the experts_implementation parameter, which includes three expert backends:

The grouped_mm backend is the key training optimization: instead of looping over experts one by one, it sorts tokens by their assigned expert and executes a single fused grouped matrix multiplication.

NeMo AutoModel takes this further. For models with custom implementations, it uses DeepEP fused all-to-all dispatch combined with grouped GEMM kernels and TransformerEngine linear layers. The progression looks like:

In NeMo AutoModel, the expert backend is configured through BackendConfig:

Transformers v5 also ships an Expert Parallelism path. It shards expert weights across GPUs. The GroupedGemmParallel style loads only each device's local experts, and RouterParallel routes tokens and combines results with an all_reduce. It's neatly built on v5's existing tensor-parallel machinery. Enabling it makes the model's tp_plan return its expert plan, so expert parallelism shares the device budget with data parallelism (ep × dp = world_size). For the single-node 30B benchmarks here, we found plain data-parallel v5 (dp=8, ep=1) to be the fastest v5 configuration, so that's the v5 setup we report.

NeMo AutoModel takes a complementary approach tuned for multi-GPU MoE training. It makes EP its own parallelism dimension, a dedicated moe_mesh alongside (rather than carved from) the data-parallel mesh, using PyTorch's DTensor with Shard(0). Because the expert mesh is orthogonal to data parallelism, the two compose on the same devices. On 8 GPUs NeMo AutoModel runs ep=8 and dp=8 together, so every GPU trains on its own data shard while holding only 1/8 of the experts. Expert weights are physically sharded across GPUs along the expert dimension.

With ep_size=8 on 8 GPUs, each GPU holds only 1/8 of the expert parameters. For a model like Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B with ~55 GiB of expert weights, EP reduces the per-GPU expert footprint from ~55 GiB to ~6.8 GiB, making training possible where FSDP-only approaches run out of memory.

On top of EP, NeMo AutoModel integrates DeepEP that fuses the token routing into optimized GPU kernels, and delivers significant speedups when combined with grouped GEMM for grouped expert computation. In our large-scale MoE benchmarks, DeepEP + grouped GEMM reduced cost per iteration by 47% on the full DeepSeek V3 671B model compared to all-gather + looped expert baselines.

Transformers v5 also introduced a dynamic weight loading system through WeightConverter and WeightRenaming. This enables MoE checkpoint to be stored in fused 3D tensors for more efficient execution. The WeightConverter applies composable operations to transform checkpoint tensors on-the-fly during from_pretrained().

NeMo AutoModel is a direct consumer of this v5 API. Over 20 model types use this mechanism through MODELS_REQUIRING_TENSOR_MERGING, including Mixtral, Qwen2 MoE, Qwen3 MoE, DeepSeek V2/V3, OLMoE, and more. The conversions are fully reversible: save_pretrained() produces standard HF-format checkpoints that any downstream tool can load.

To try NeMo AutoModel, please visit our official documentation page to get started.

NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel is the natural next step for HuggingFace users scaling up model training. By building directly on Transformers v5, AutoModel provides a zero-friction upgrade path: change one import line and get a model instance that is more than three times as fast.

On Qwen3-30B-A3B and Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B, this delivers 3.4-3.7x higher training throughput with 29-32% less GPU memory compared to the best Transformers v5 configuration. And because true Expert Parallelism shards experts across GPUs, the same path scales up to full fine-tuning a 550B model like Nemotron 3 Ultra across 16 nodes, the regime where Expert Parallelism becomes essential to fit the model in memory. Because NeMo AutoModel checkpoints are standard HF-format safetensors, you can deploy them on inference frameworks like vLLM and SGLang.

The code, configs, and benchmark scripts are all available in the NeMo AutoModel repository.

Core contributors to this work, listed alphabetically by last name: Adil Asif, Hemil Desai, Alexandros Koumparoulis, and Huiying Li.

GitHub now highlights ACCESSIBILITY.md files and helps maintainers document accessibility goals, known barriers, supported environments, contributor expectations, and reporting processes.

Accessibility work often lives in issue trackers, contribution guidelines, audit reports, team knowledge, and conversations with users. When that information has no predictable home, people who encounter a barrier must search for it, and maintainers lose context as contributors and project ownership change.

An ACCESSIBILITY.md file, now visible on repository overview pages, gives a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers.

GitHub now recognizes the ACCESSIBILITY.md file in the repository’s root, .github/ directory, or docs/ directory. A repository can also inherit a statement from its organization’s .github/ repository. For public repositories, maintainers can add or propose a statement from Insights > Community Standards using a concise starter document.

GitHub’s community health files help people understand how a project works:

Recognizing ACCESSIBILITY.md gives accessibility information a dedicated place alongside that guidance.

New repositories also include an accessibility issue label by default. The statement explains how to report a barrier and what to expect next, while the label helps maintainers organize and track the resulting work.

GitHub CLI’s accessibility statement, for example, documents settings, known barriers, and workarounds. It explains why table output can be difficult to follow with a screen reader and provides a command that prints pull request numbers and titles one per line instead. It also asks contributors changing prompts or output to show the results with relevant accessibility settings enabled. Developers using the CLI get a specific workaround; developers contributing to it get clear expectations for their changes.

The GitHub Annotation Toolkit’s accessibility statement documents a limitation of its Figma library: annotations use canvas position, connecting lines, and matching numbers to visually convey relationships. Access to individual canvas objects does not necessarily communicate what those relationships are.

The statement gives collaborators a concrete alternative: provide a structured text description that identifies each annotated element, its intended semantics and behavior, and any relevant ordering. For developers preparing or receiving a design handoff, this explains what information needs to accompany the visual annotations.

The file also explains how to report accessibility barriers and explicitly states that the library has not undergone keyboard-only or screen-reader testing. Readers get both practical guidance and clear limits on what the project has verified. Showing this information in the repository overview makes it easier to find alongside the project’s other documentation.

There is no one fixed format for an ACCESSIBILITY.md file. A small library, command-line tool, documentation site, and large web application have different users, risks, and maintenance capacity. Start with accurate information that the project can keep current.

Keep in mind that a project can name a Web Content Accessibility Guidelines version and level as a target. A target does not establish verified conformance. A conformance claim requires an evaluation and should identify the evaluated scope, date, method, and evaluator.

The most useful accessibility statements serve people who arrive after something has already gone wrong. Plain language, descriptive links, and a clear reporting route matter more than legal or standards-heavy language.

Useful reporting guidance invites relevant context, such as the affected task, page, observed behavior, browser, operating system, and assistive technology. It makes screenshots and recordings optional and avoids asking someone to prove a disability.

The statement should also set expectations that maintainers can consistently meet. That can include acknowledgement, status updates, available workarounds, expected timelines, and an opportunity for the reporter to verify a fix.

The Open Source Accessibility Toolkit provides a detailed public example.

GitHub’s Community Standards workflow provides a shorter starter with prompts that projects can replace with their own information. The goal is not to produce a perfect policy before publishing the file. Start with accurate information, name the gaps, and update the statement as the project’s accessibility practices mature.

Adding an accessibility statement makes accessibility work more discoverable to users, contributors, and maintainers. Normalizing that practice across open source projects helps make accessibility part of how communities plan, build, report, and improve their work.

Add an accessibility statement to your repository >

Jan Maarten (he/him) is a designer and accessibility specialist living on unceded Duwamish lands. He brings two decades of experience across product design, brand, strategy, and leadership. At GitHub, he bridges design and engineering to improve accessible products, evolve design-system infrastructure, and create resources for the wider design community, including the open-source GitHub Annotation Toolkit.

GitHub’s new Git storage architecture is built so thousands of agents can push to a single repository at once. Here’s how it works.

Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running.

Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post, we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage.

We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. Virtual replicas were the first step toward building around that, and the means by which we onboard repositories to the new architecture.

The rest of the architecture builds on that observation. Only reference updates need agreement. That lets the parts of Git infrastructure that used to be tightly coupled (storing data, serving requests, and maintaining repositories) scale independently. For developers, Git stays Git: they push, fetch, and branch the same way, with the same protections in place. Below, we walk through the requirements behind the design, follow a request through the system, and dive deep into two of its components.

We think about the scale of the GitHub platform along two axes:

Today, the busiest repositories on GitHub.com receive at most dozens of writes in a single second, typically in short bursts. As more of that work shifts to agents running in parallel and around the clock, we expect those bursts to become a sustained rate within the next year. Each push leads to more reads: CI runs, deployment systems pull the new commit, and other agents fetch it for context. This read fan-out results in a large amplification effect on overall traffic that scales with writes.

We’re already seeing this trend play out on repositories at the top of the curve. The chart below shows daily requests to one repository on GitHub from March to May, when its traffic grew about 4x. Its growth has continued on an exponential trajectory since then.

We have to plan for a world where agent-driven development keeps accelerating at this speed. Instead of planning for the next increment, we set a target of at least two orders of magnitude more scale. For a single repository, that meant the new architecture needed to:

On top of that, the system had to be able to improve overall reliability and scale globally.

In May of 2026, hot on the heels of the initial Azure migration, we started working on a design that could meet those demands. We tried several approaches. In all of them, pack data lived in Azure Blob Storage, and in some we experimented with keeping reference state there too. We’ll cover some of the trade-offs we found below, but we settled on a design we felt maximized throughput while preserving the correctness, durability, availability, and latency guarantees a platform like GitHub requires. We called it “Rubicon,” a nod to the point of no return the industry crossed with agentic development.

Let’s walk through Rubicon from the top down. Many things stay the same: requests from Git clients, the API, and the web UI arrive at Spokes, which still handles routing and load balancing, and serves the internal API that the rest of GitHub uses to read and write repository data. Spokes also maintains its role as a placement and balancing service, maintaining the partitioning, isolation, and tenant fairness required for horizontal scale. The data plane underneath Spokes, in contrast, is new.

Spokes routes each request to one of a small group of virtual replicas assigned to that repository. Virtual replicas are a single fleet of disposable compute that serves reads, writes, or both. A virtual replica’s local disk is a cache that can be rebuilt at any time.

Spokes routes a repository’s traffic to the same virtual replicas when it can, which keeps their caches warm and latency low, but nothing about correctness depends on a request landing on any particular virtual replica. When a virtual replica goes away, the repository’s other virtual replicas keep serving, and a replacement fills its cache as traffic arrives.

When a repository gets busy, we add more virtual replicas. Separately, a fleet of compaction nodes works in the background, directly against Blob Storage and Ref-CAS, to merge each repository’s packs and remove unreachable objects. That work never runs on a virtual replica, meaning their CPU and memory can be almost entirely dedicated to serving requests.

Let’s walk the architecture from the perspective of a write and a read:

There are many distinct approaches we’ve taken within the new architecture, from the software stack on the virtual replicas to how traffic routing and workload scheduling are tuned for different use cases (e.g., many small repos vs. one large one). Let’s dive deep into two components of the architecture and tell their stories centered on the two design principles.

Object storage services like Azure Blob Storage are incredibly good at what they do, and natural fits for many data-heavy applications like source code storage. They are durable and replicated, hold as much as we need them to, have a relatively low cost per byte, and deliver exceptionally high aggregate throughput so long as traffic is spread across many keys. As a result, nearly everything durable in the new Git storage architecture lives in Azure Blob Storage, including:

Most of that data is written once to a distinct key and never changes afterward, which is what makes it highly suitable for Blob Storage.

References are the opposite. A busy repository’s references are a relatively small piece of state that many writes race to update at the same time. That access pattern is harder to serve from Blob Storage, and our first prototypes showed us why. Object storage for this kind of workload is an intuitive choice, and one that works well up to a certain level of scale: conditional writes give a compare-and-swap for free, and the data is already durable and replicated. However, we ran into a difficult set of choices, illustrated below by two approaches we tried.

Our first approach was a write-ahead log for all of a repository’s references, indexed by a single blob. Every update is a conditional write against that blob. It’s correct, and reads are cheap: a virtual replica asks whether the blob has changed, and if it hasn’t, it’s done. Writes are where it falls short. Only one conditional write to a blob can be in flight at a time, so even when we batch every push that arrives during a write into the next one, the repository’s write ceiling is one write per round trip to a single blob. In practice, this netted us write throughput in the mid-hundreds per second.

Our second approach split the references across several segment blobs, with each reference hashing to one of them. Writes to references in different segments no longer wait on each other, which raises the ceiling. But a read now has to check every segment to know whether anything changed, and it’s only as fast as the slowest segment. We’d traded write latency for read latency, and reads outnumber writes by orders of magnitude. We can visualize this by showing multiple writes and a read side by side:

Neither option met every requirement, so we built something else: a replicated log service dedicated to references, or the Ref-CAS service. This is the (small) consensus group we said at the end of the last post was still somewhere in the stack. Here’s how it works.

Each reference update in Ref-CAS is a compare-and-swap committed by a quorum. A transaction locks only the references it touches, checks that each one still has the value the writer expects, and becomes visible once a majority of the log’s replicas have recorded it. Agents mostly push to their own branches, so most updates don’t contend, and they replicate in parallel. When two pushes do update the same reference, only one will append to the log.

Each commit to Ref-CAS gets a log sequence number (LSN), and the repository’s version is the LSN of its latest commit. Reads start with a version check against that version. A virtual replica sends the version of the reference state it already holds. If that version is still current, the reply carries no references at all, and an unchanged repository costs a single comparison. If the virtual replica is behind, it gets back the current references and version, along with pointers to pack data and anything else that needs to be known, such as when the last garbage collection cycle occurred.

Unlike the consensus group in our legacy architecture, Ref-CAS never holds or validates object data. It only stores pointers to it. A virtual replica uploads a push’s pack to Blob Storage before it commits the reference transaction. A reference only ever points at objects that are already durable.

These approaches allow us to transact reference state alone in the tens of thousands of operations per second, and provide a baseline for additional annotations on the replication log that help reads decide what to download for a given request.

But supporting thousands of writes per second on a single repository creates a second-order problem: maintaining the performance of reads and writes. For that, we needed a different approach to compaction.

Every push adds a pack to Blob Storage. Git can serve a repository from many packs, but each additional pack makes lookups slightly more expensive, so the pack count can’t grow without bound. In our legacy architecture, compaction runs on the same replicas that serve traffic, and it has to run on every replica. In the new architecture, it runs entirely in the background on separate nodes, directly against durable storage, using the Ref-CAS service to notify virtual replicas of the evolving state.

Compaction nodes each claim ownership over a subset of the repository’s data via a lease, which allows us to scale compaction horizontally. Here’s how one compaction node works through a single shard of a repository’s packs:

The node first takes a lease on the shard in Blob Storage, so only one node compacts a shard at a time. Meanwhile, virtual replicas keep uploading packs and listing them in the pack manifest. The node reads the manifest to find new packs and collects them into an open segment, which is effectively a holding ground for data about to be compacted. When the segment reaches a defined limit based on pack count, size, or age, it seals the segment so it accepts no new packs, then combines its packs into fewer, larger ones. While compaction happens, the next segment for the shard can begin capturing its input packs. Before anything is published, the node checks that the new packs contain exactly the same objects as the inputs. It then uploads the new packs and adds them to the manifest. A second transaction removes the inputs from the manifest, and cleanup deletes them later.

To scale out, this process runs independently for many shards at once. Each pack’s hash maps to a shard, so adding shards and nodes adds compaction throughput. A compacted pack that’s still under the size limit goes back into a shard by its own hash and merges again, so packs grow in tiers until they reach the limit. The net result is an effectively flat pack count while pushes climb:

Compaction merges packs, but it keeps every object. Garbage collection is the step that removes objects nothing references anymore, like the ones left behind by deleted branches and force-pushes. In our new architecture, garbage collection works very similarly to compaction by using dedicated workers to handle the compute-heavy portion. It also has a few special behaviors for safely removing data, which are worthy of their own discussion.

Using these approaches, we’ve been able to consistently demonstrate a flat latency curve as writes climb, and we have other planned optimizations to make the compaction and garbage collection processes themselves more performant.

The two principles we started with let each part of this architecture scale on its own. We scale reads and writes by adding virtual replicas. Ref-CAS orders each reference independently instead of the whole repository. We scale maintenance by adding compaction nodes. Our goal is for every repository, from one developer’s side project to the busiest monorepo, to run on the same architecture with no special handling for the busy ones. Repositories don’t stay small. A side project can pick up a fleet of agents overnight, and it shouldn’t need a migration or special handling from us to keep up. One architecture also means every improvement we make reaches every repository at once.

This foundation lets us do a lot more. We’re focused on three areas next: scaling the architecture beyond what we can predict we’ll need today, making agents more efficient at the work they do on GitHub, and evolving Git itself for agentic development.

We have plans to take this architecture further. Each of these improvements lets a repository handle more activity while reducing the work behind each request:

Scaling the infrastructure is one side of supporting agents. The other side is making each agent operation cheaper: fewer bytes to fetch, fewer round trips, and less waiting on changes. Each of these fast-follow items builds on the storage work in this post:

We also have work to do in Git itself. GitHub has been a longtime contributor to the Git project, and we’re not stopping now. A few examples of the work we’re excited to continue:

Agents have changed how software gets built. GitHub and Git are changing with it. We’re excited to take this new architecture across the starting line. It’s available in a limited private preview now, with a broader rollout early next year. We can’t wait to see what teams build when the number of agents working on a repository is limited by their ideas. We’ll keep evolving Git and GitHub alongside our customers and the Git community.

Brian is a Principal Software Engineer working on the storage and core services that power all repository interactions on GitHub.

#10022. Run a vLLM Server on HF Jobs in One Command

You can spin up a private, OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint on Hugging Face infrastructure with a single command — no servers to provision, no Kubernetes, pay-per-second. Once it's up, you can query it from your laptop, a notebook, or anywhere else.

It's the quickest way to stand up a model for tests, evals, or batch generation. (If you're after a managed, production-ready service instead, that's what Inference Endpoints are for — more on when to pick which at the end.)

hf jobs run is docker run for HF infrastructure. We use the official vllm/vllm-openai image, ask for a GPU with --flavor, and expose vLLM's port with --expose:

--expose 8000 routes the container's port through HF's public jobs proxy (see the Serve Models guide for the full reference). The command prints the URL your server is reachable at:

6a381ca1953ed90bfb947332 is your job ID. Keep track of it, we'll need it. We'll use as a placeholder for it in the rest of the post.

Give it a couple of minutes to download weights and boot. When the logs show Application startup complete, you're live.

vLLM speaks the OpenAI API, and every request just needs your HF token as a bearer token. The quickest way to hit it is curl:

which returns the usual OpenAI-style JSON, with choices[0].message.content holding "Hello! How can I assist you today? 😊".

Or, from Python, point the OpenAI client at the exposed URL and pass the token as the API key:

Quick health check before you start: curl https://--8000.hf.jobs/v1/models -H "Authorization: Bearer $(hf auth token)" should list the model.

🔐 The endpoint is gated, not public. Every request must carry an HF token with read access to the job's namespace. A plain browser visit will be rejected. In effect, the jobs proxy is your API gate: access is scoped to you (and your org). That's fine for private use, but treat the URL accordingly: don't share it expecting it to be open, and don't paste your token into untrusted places. If you need finer-grained or public access, put a proper gateway in front instead. Or see HF Jobs or Inference Endpoints? below.

Jobs are billed per second, so stop the server when you're done:

The --timeout you set is a safety net (it'll auto-stop), but cancelling explicitly is cheaper. An a10g-large runs at $1.50/hour — check hf jobs hardware for the full price list and pick the smallest flavor that fits your model.

The same command scales to much larger models — pick a beefier --flavor and tell vLLM to shard the model across the GPUs with --tensor-parallel-size. For example, the 122B Qwen3.5 mixture-of-experts model on 2× H200:

--tensor-parallel-size should match the number of GPUs in the flavor (h200x2 → 2, h200x8 → 8). Run hf jobs hardware to see what's available and give bigger models a longer --timeout, since they take longer to download and load. For large models, H200 flavors are usually the best value.

The --max-model-len 32768 --max-num-seqs 256 flags are specific to this model: Qwen3.5-122B is a hybrid Mamba/attention architecture with a 256K-token default context, which doesn't leave enough memory for vLLM's default batch settings. Capping the context length and concurrent-sequence count keeps it within the GPUs' memory. If a model fails to start with an out-of-memory or cache-block error, dialing these two down is the first thing to try. Everything else (the exposed URL, the OpenAI client, the token auth) stays exactly the same.

Prefer a chat window over curl? A few lines of Gradio point at the same endpoint. Add --reasoning-parser deepseek_r1 to the vllm serve command so Qwen3's thinking comes back as a separate field (not necessary, but helpful), then run this code locally (you'll just need the job ID):

Run it, open http://127.0.0.1:7860, and chat — reasoning streams into the collapsible panel, the answer below.

Need to debug a startup failure, watch GPU memory, or tail logs interactively? You can open a shell straight into the running job. Launch it with --ssh and make sure your public key is registered at huggingface.co/settings/keys:

You're now inside the container, where you can run nvidia-smi, inspect the process, or poke at the model directly — which makes debugging and monitoring much easier than reading logs from the outside. SSH support requires huggingface_hub >= 1.20.0.

The same endpoint can back a terminal coding agent. Pi is a provider-agnostic agent harness. Point it at the job and you get a Read/Write/Edit/Bash agent running on your own self-hosted model.

One thing to set up first: agents drive the model through tool calls, and vLLM only accepts those if the server is launched with tool calling enabled. So relaunch with --enable-auto-tool-choice and a --tool-call-parser matching the model family (hermes for Qwen3). Agents also benefit from a stronger model, so this is a good place to bring in the bigger one:

Then add the job as a custom provider in ~/.pi/agent/models.json:

The model you spun up a couple of commands ago, now driving an interactive coding agent in your terminal.

HF Jobs isn't the only way to serve a model on Hugging Face. Inference Endpoints are our managed product for the same job, and which one fits depends on what you're after.

Reach for HF Jobs when you want maximum flexibility and control: it's just docker run on HF infrastructure, so you pick the image, the exact vllm serve flags, and the hardware, and you pay per second for as long as the job runs. That makes it a great fit for experiments, one-off evals, batch generation, or kicking the tires on a model before committing to anything.

Reach for Inference Endpoints when you want something more production-ready. They add the operational niceties a long-lived service needs: finer-grained access control (an endpoint can be public, protected, or private), and scale-to-zero, so you're not billed during periods of inactivity. If you're standing up a durable endpoint rather than running a job, that's the tool to grab.

This post sticks to vLLM, but the same expose-a-port pattern works with any OpenAI-compatible server. To serve GGUFs with llama.cpp or run SGLang instead, see the Serve Models on Jobs guide, which walks through those backends.

#10021. 3AM Affiliate Embraces AI-Like Loops in European School Attack

Evidence suggests a model may have generated and revised commands during the ransom gang's breach, though researchers stopped short of claiming full automation.

A 3AM ransomware attack targeting a UK school estate may provide an early look at how cybercriminals could use AI as a force multiplier rather than a replacement for human operators.

Bitdefender today published research concerning a "hybrid AI ransomware attack" observed in the wild, attributing certain actions taken to human or agentic elements. On the surface, the attack is fairly straightforward. As a blog post explained, a 3AM ransomware affiliate attacked a school in the UK, "then used ordinary Windows tools to build domain trusts and reach other schools."

Attackers stole backup credentials, created rogue domain-admin accounts, established trusts between previously separate Active Directory domains, moved between schools, stole data, and deployed 3AM ransomware. In other words, the attack largely followed a familiar ransomware playbook, despite Bitdefender's claims that AI helped execute parts of the operation.

Related:'AdFection' Turns Ad Impressions Into Zero-Click Spyware Delivery

Where the attack got more interesting was how, as the security vendor argued, it didn't fit neatly into pre-existing buckets for attacks involving AI. It wasn't exactly an AI-generated attack where the malware was fully or largely created by a large language model (LLM); it wasn't exactly an AI-assisted attack where human engineers built the tools while using AI to speed up work; and it wasn't exactly an AI-operated attack where the LLM orchestrates actions and runs the show, as it were.

In this case, Bitdefender argued an AI system appeared to handle repetitive command generation and troubleshooting while a human operator made high-level decisions.

Many elements of the attack were ordinary for ransomware, such as significant use of living-off-the-land (LOTL) techniques, where attackers abuse tools already present on the victim's machine rather than relying on malware — in this case PowerShell, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI), reg, netsh, rundll32, and other domain and scheduling utilities preinstalled on Windows. The attacker also used "an Impacket-style remote-execution tool," as well as Mimikatz and a previously published Veeam script.

But despite the attack's ordinary nature, Bitdefender assessed that several things suggest the use of an agentic loop, the control structure that makes an AI agent work. Certain actions appeared to be taken by a program rather than a human operator.

"The commands carry the usual tells of a model: a call to the backup software's web interface (Veeam, a widely used enterprise backup product) on a port and with a login method that do not match the vendor’s documentation, a mistake typical of writing from memory rather than from the manual (Veeam REST API authorization), along with confirmation files, self-labeled output and numbered revisions of the same script," the blog post read. "The retries behave like a loop too."

Related:Biomemory Launches DNA Shield, First Commercial Product Built on Its Molecular IT Platform

In another example, researchers assessed that the time taken between PowerShell command attempts was shorter than a human would take if issuing them by hand, but longer than if an LLM was orchestrating by itself. The longer time taken between individual tasks but the shorter time between retries "is what it looks like if a person is choosing the next step and a model is handling the retries."

Bitdefender caveated its findings by noting that it was unable to access the machine the attacker worked from, so it couldn't document anything tangible involving the AI model itself. The research acts as an argument that this attack behaves like a human operating alongside an agent, which is a working model defenders may wish to plan around.

With that in mind, Martin Zugec, technical solutions director at Bitdefender, tells Dark Reading that "a hybrid model is more reasonable for financially motivated cybercriminals, technically and economically, than a fully autonomous attack."

Related:Foul Language: WordlistLoader Disguises Malware as Ordinary Text

But even as a one-off, the situation is notable because the primary victim was an organization in a critical sector, and Bitdefender's anecdote suggests the affiliate may have used an AI agent to scale the attack by handling repetitive troubleshooting and command generation, although the report stops short of showing AI-enabled capabilities the attacker otherwise lacked.

Moreover, other similar institutions could fall in the crosshairs. "From a domain controller it enumerated trust relationships between domains and searched SYSVOL (the shared folder where Active Directory stores logon scripts, readable by any domain user) for the names and subnets of other schools," according to the research blog post.

The good news is that because much of this attack followed the typical ransomware playbook, the defender recommendations that stop regular ransomware would also stop the attack described in this research.

Zugec adds that agentic loops are noisy from an indicator standpoint, as many of their actions are repetitive and brute force in nature. "An agentic loop doesn’t make an attack quiet; it makes it repetitive: the same command re-run, small tweaks, numbered scripts and probe files left on disk. Even the quickest retries took 40 seconds or more. 'Machine speed' is mostly a marketing phrase about very expensive incidents; in real attacks, especially with local models, we expect this slower and noisier pattern. Speed isn't the giveaway; repetition is."

The vendor recommends focusing on prevention: Keep admin credentials of different domains separate, treat backups as a possible target, restrict remote execution and administrative shares to known management hosts, block interpreters and shells on machines that never use them, and put endpoint security tooling on every machine.

"Prefer controls that work regardless of volume and speed," the blog post read, "because they stop an action the first time and the hundredth."
