#10006. DigiCert admits 16-month security lapse exposed customer information

Botched server move left the door open, and DigiCert took months to notice someone had wandered in

DigiCert has admitted that a botched server migration left an internal system exposed to the internet for more than a year, allowing an unauthorized user to access customer data, including passports, driver's licenses, and other identity documents.

The certificate authority has begun notifying affected customers but has yet to disclose how many people had their information exposed.

In an email seen by The Register, DigiCert confirmed the compromised information included names, business email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses. Some records may also have contained passports, driver's licenses, utility bills, or other identification documents.

"We are completing a review of identification documents to determine the specific individuals involved," DigiCert told those affected, adding that it would notify those people once the review was complete.

DigiCert's incident report traces the blunder back to February 2025, when an internal business system was moved from a VPN-protected network to a different availability zone. That change also opened the system up to the public internet, where it sat for more than 16 months without DigiCert realizing.

The archive used the same account management platform as DigiCert's customer-facing products, including a self-registration feature that was never supposed to be available on the internal system. This allowed outsiders to create accounts without multifactor authentication and, thanks to a separate permissions flaw, use them to browse archived customer records.

DigiCert found the unauthorized accounts on June 18, 2026, but initially dismissed them as harmless because they weren't assigned to an application. A security researcher raised the alarm about the account creation issue three days later, but it took until July 2 for DigiCert to shut it down.

Unfortunately, someone had already been poking around.

It wasn't until October 12 that DigiCert began investigating whether customer information had actually been accessed. On October 19, it confirmed that an unauthorized account had accessed a subset of archived records between June 27 and July 2.

DigiCert described the affected records as a "small proportion" of its archive but hasn't disclosed how many customers or individuals were caught up in the breach. The company did not respond to The Register’s questions at the time of publication.

DigiCert's postmortem makes for uncomfortable reading. The server move didn't get a proper security review, monitoring failed to pick up suspicious activity, and the access controls weren't much use against self-registered accounts. The company has since switched off self-registration, tightened network access, and added monitoring that might have come in handy a few months earlier.

Certificate authority operations, CertCentral, and DigiCert ONE were unaffected, the company said, adding that customer credentials and issued certificates remain secure. It also found no evidence that the unauthorized account had been used to issue, revoke, or validate certificates.

That’s good news for anyone worried about their certificates, but less so for those who handed DigiCert a copy of their passport. ®

#10004. PRX Part 4: Our Data Strategy

Welcome back! This is Part 4 of the PRX series. Parts 1 to 3 covered model architectures, training design, and a 24-hour speedrun. This time we're pulling back the curtain on the part that quietly underpins all of it: the data. Of all the things that shaped PRX's quality, the data pipeline was one of the least glamorous parts to build but nevertheless an important piece to get right. Here's what we did, what we'd do differently, and a few things we only learned the slow way.

In one sentence: we assemble training data from a mix of public and internal datasets, re-caption the images with a VLM, and turn the result into the streamable corpus we trained PRX on.

At a high level, the data pipeline looks like this:

In the following we will dive into it in detail.

The goal was to assemble a large, diverse dataset for pre-training. At this stage the model is learning how the world looks: the visual concepts, the objects and scenes, how things are composed and lit, and the sheer range of what images can contain. That is a problem of coverage and diversity, not of per-image perfection. A broad, representative corpus teaches the model far more about the structure of the visual world than a smaller, prettier one would, even if many of the individual images are ordinary snapshots or slightly compressed. Over-filtering for aesthetics at this stage would actually hurt, narrowing the distribution and costing the model concepts and compositional variety it cannot recover later. Making generations look polished is a separate, later concern, which we leave to fine-tuning and preference alignment on small, ruthlessly curated sets. Pre-training is for breadth; fine-tuning is for taste.

We assemble our pre-training data from a mix of public and internal datasets. The priority at this stage is breadth, diversity, and standing on curation that already exists rather than redoing it ourselves. Where a source already comes quality-filtered, deduplicated, and filtered for NSFW content and personal information, we build on that work instead of repeating it at scale. Sources arrive in different shapes: some come with the image data itself, others as metadata plus baseline captions that we bring into a common form. We took a pragmatic approach: rather than build a corpus entirely from scratch, we leaned on existing datasets and our own tooling to assemble one quickly. In hindsight it is not necessarily the absolute best dataset one could build, but it was a solid and lightweight starting point for pre-training a 7B model.

In our experience, what matters most for pre-training is to use long captions that accurately describe everything in the image. We saw this directly in Part 2, where switching from short captions to long ones substantially improved sample quality. If captioning is faithful, we don't need to worry about the occasional screenshot, advertisement, logo, or bit of text in an image, because those things get described in the caption too, so the model learns them as conditioned, controllable attributes rather than reproducing them unconditionally. Accurate captioning turns "noise" into something you can prompt for, or prompt away. This is precisely why the filtering we do later is deliberately light. We remove what is genuinely unusable, not everything that is imperfect.

We have been using Mosaic Streaming and Mosaic Data Shards (MDS) as a dataset format for distributed training for a while now. In combination with Mosaic Composer we found it to be a very low-maintenance, flexible, and well-performing framework for distributed training. Furthermore, MDS datasets can easily and effectively be mixed and shuffled and also allow for distributed training directly from object storage like S3 or GCS.

However, MDS datasets are very rigid. Adding a column or creating a subset for a given filter basically means that one has to scan and rewrite the whole dataset. That's why we use Lance for this kind of feature engineering and dataset curation. Lance is a columnar data format with cheap predicate pushdown, scalar indexes, and vector search, the right tool for building and exploring datasets with billions of rows.

These two formats play off each other throughout this post and the PRX data pipeline: Lance to build, MDS to stream.

For previous training runs, we used T5Gemma as the text encoder and pre-computed the text latents, storing them in MDS as bytes. This time around, after switching the text encoder to Qwen3-VL, we decided to compute text latents on the fly during training instead. Running the text encoder inside the training loop costs throughput, but how much depends on the model: for a small denoiser it can be significant, whereas at PRX's 7B scale the text encoder's compute is negligible next to the denoiser, and we measured only a roughly 3–4% throughput cost (about 1 extra day on a 30-day run). In return we get two things. Skipping pre-computation keeps our MDS shards much smaller, small enough to store the full pre-training dataset on the SSD-backed shared filesystem of our SLURM cluster rather than streaming it over the network from object storage. And it keeps us free to change the text encoder later without rewriting terabytes of stored latents, which is exactly the kind of switch we made when moving to Qwen3-VL.

We encoded all images as JPEG at quality 92, instead of a lossless format such as PNG. We did not just assume quality 92 was safe, we measured it. Real-world images have usually already been JPEG-compressed several times, so the real question is whether one more re-encode hurts. Across repeated decode/encode cycles on both high-resolution (1–2 MP) and lower-resolution (0.25–0.5 MP) real images, the first re-encode at quality 92 is essentially imperceptible. Each further cycle adds almost nothing, because JPEG quickly converges to a stable state, and even after 10 cycles the images stay well within the imperceptible range, while PNG would be 3–10× larger for no perceptual gain. The numbers, averaged over 100 images at quality 92 and measured against the original (higher PSNR and lower LPIPS are better):

Since most source images already arrive JPEG-compressed, storing them losslessly as PNG buys little, so we convert everything to JPEG at high quality (quality 92).

We also checked what matters most: whether training on JPEGs changes what the model produces. Our corpus is mostly JPEG anyway, so the only advantage PNG could offer is not introducing new artifacts. We deliberately drew the comparison from high-resolution sources, on the expectation that even originally-JPEG images carry few artifacts at high resolution. We trained two identical PRX models at 1024px on the same images, one stored as PNG and one as JPEG at quality 92. Both trained equally well on our metrics, and their generations were practically indistinguishable, including when we estimated how JPEG-compressed the outputs look using a known technique for estimating JPEG quality by matching quantization tables:

The detection rate is the fraction of generations in which any quantization structure is found at all. The mean and median estimated JPEG quality are taken over only those flagged images. The two models are practically indistinguishable: only about one generation in ten from either shows any detectable quantization structure, and the differences are small enough that we are confident the training image format has a minimal effect on output quality. So high-quality JPEG storage adds nothing measurable on top of what the sources already carry. For large-scale text-to-image training that is more than good enough. For artifact-sensitive data used to train other Photoroom models, such as our custom AI Shadows model, we still rely on PNGs.

You cannot interactively explore Parquet tables with hundreds of millions or even billions of rows. We therefore store the data in Lance, where we can index, query, and browse it. We run the ingest with Ray Data, reading the source tables in parallel and writing many fragments of a Lance table across the cluster.

One lesson worth sharing is about fragmentation. A Lance table is split into fragments, and several operations scale with the total number of fragments rather than the row count: a scan opens the files of every fragment, and some metadata operations are O(number of fragments). A table broken into too many small fragments therefore queries slowly no matter its size. The Lance performance guidance is to keep that count low (the rule of thumb is on the order of a hundred fragments even for a billion-row table) and to run compaction periodically to merge small fragments into larger ones.

We learned this the slow way. Our first ingest targeted only 100,000 rows per fragment, which left thousands of tiny fragments and made even simple filters and full-text queries crawl. After compacting up to roughly a million rows per fragment, which for our tables of several hundred million rows meant on the order of a thousand fragments, queries were fast and we stopped worrying about it. The right target depends on row width, query patterns, and how the data is written, and in hindsight fewer, larger fragments might have been a better default. Lance supports distributed compaction (for example via the Lance-Ray integration), so it is easy to adjust after the fact, but it pays not to over-fragment in the first place.

We chose to re-caption every image ourselves rather than rely on the captions some of the datasets happened to ship with. The reason is consistency: across a mix of sources, caption length, style, and quality vary a lot, and we wanted a single uniform standard across the whole corpus (more on the captioner in Section 3).

The metadata a dataset already carries is still valuable, though, just for a different purpose. Pre-existing captions, and the vector embeddings that sometimes come alongside them (for example CLIP embeddings), are what make a dataset explorable in Lance right away: full-text search over the captions and nearest-neighbor search over an embedding column let us navigate the data and quickly judge its quality and the filtering it will need, well before we have run our own captioning over it. So we keep both, joining them in when they live in a separate table, and lean on them for the browsing we describe next.

With the data queryable, we could quickly profile it. The resolution distribution, for example, told us where to set cutoffs. Our smallest training bucket is 512² pixels, and we cap upscaling into a bucket at 4/3 (about 33%), so the effective cutoff is 384² ≈ 147k pixels plus an aspect ratio in [0.5, 2.0]. Everything below that we discard.

Lance tables support full-text search on text columns as well as nearest-neighbor similarity search on vector embedding columns out of the box, and both can be accelerated by building indexes. We did exactly that for the caption and embedding columns, then built a small UI to browse the dataset: real-time text search over the captions as well as navigating clusters of visually similar images via vector search.

Browsing the data this way let us assess its diversity and quality qualitatively and spot issues early, simply by looking at it. We found uninformative baseline captions, a surprising amount of non-photographic content (screenshots, slides, documents, infographics), and some near-duplicate images. These observations shaped the rest of the pipeline directly: re-caption everything (longer, accurate captions describe even imperfect images well, and guarantee that the caption matches the exact image we train on), and add light filtering and deduplication passes later. In general, we believe this sort of exploration tool is invaluable for getting a feel for a dataset before committing to it.

We found that long, detailed captions are a very strong lever on output quality. In an early benchmark we trained a small diffusion model twice on the same images, once on captions we generated with Qwen2.5-VL-7B and once on much shorter captions (produced with LLaVA-1.5-LLaMA3-8B), and scored both over training. The long captions generated with Qwen2.5-VL-7B won across the board, with lower FID, CMMD, and DINO-MMD at every checkpoint (lower is better on all three).

A small diffusion model trained on Qwen2.5-VL-7B captions (red) versus the baseline LLaVA-1.5-LLaMA3-8B captions (blue), scored every 10k steps up to 100k. Lower is better on all three metrics.

Here is an example image with both our long, VLM-generated caption as well as the shorter caption used as the baseline:

Our captioning runs as a streaming pipeline built on Ray Data: it reads the data from Lance, prepares each image, captions it on the GPU, and writes the caption back as a new column we can query and filter on. We prompt for a single dense, visually grounded paragraph rather than a one-line caption.

A tight schedule and limited resources meant that we couldn't spend too much time on ablations of different captioning models and system prompts.

We used the following prompts to generate the captions.

We shortlisted three VLMs as captioner candidates:

We benchmarked caption quality indirectly: we trained a small diffusion model for 100k steps on each caption variant and scored its generations with FID, CMMD, and DINO-MMD. Alongside the three candidates we scored two reference captioners, to connect this comparison to the first benchmark: the base Qwen2.5-VL-7B (the same model as in the benchmark above) and a set of Gemini 1.5 Flash captions we had generated earlier for the 1M-image internal test set used here. The Gemini captions are a similar length but were produced with a different prompt (all others use the system prompt above), so its curve is indicative rather than a like-for-like comparison.

FID, CMMD, and DINO-MMD over training for the three captioner candidates and two reference captioners, scored every 10k steps up to 100k. Lower is better on all three.

Among the candidates, Qwen3.5-9B is best on all three metrics, with Qwen3-VL-8B close behind on FID and DINO-MMD (though weaker on CMMD) and the Relaxed captioner trailing on FID but competitive elsewhere. The clearest result is that the base Qwen2.5-VL-7B — the same model that beat the baseline in the first benchmark — is now the weakest of the five, which is exactly why we didn't just keep it: a caption-tuned or newer model measurably helps. (Gemini 1.5 Flash lands mid-pack, but with the different-prompt caveat above.)

We put less weight on throughput than quality, but at hundreds of millions of images it still matters, since it sets how much the captions cost to generate. We measured it only for the three candidates, all served through vLLM with no quantization or custom kernels. The tuning was at the pipeline level: one vLLM replica per GPU, with enough Ray Data pool workers to keep all eight GPUs on a node saturated. We first found Qwen3-VL-8B to be the fastest (20 img/s per H200) and chose it, for its speed, quality, and stable, release-grade vLLM support. Only later did we find that the Qwen2.5-VL "Relaxed" captioner reaches the same 20 img/s once fixed: it had been saved with the wrong architecture class, which broke vLLM's torch.compile hashing and forced slow eager mode until we re-saved it as Qwen2_5_VLForConditionalGeneration. Qwen3.5-9B produces great captions but ran slower (~6.5 img/s) and needed unstable nightly dependency builds at the time. A few months on, it is probably a great choice too.

At the end of the pipeline, we turn the captioned, bucketed stream into MDS, the format the trainer streams.

The Mosaic Streaming library packs samples into ~128MB shards streamed during training from object storage or a local filesystem. Lance does support simple distributed training as well, but we found that converting to MDS is the lower friction path for us. Mosaic Streaming gives us, for free, the distributed-training machinery we'd otherwise have to build ourselves:

Diffusion training runs on fixed-size tensors, so every image in a batch must share one width and height. Rather than crop everything square (losing the sides of portraits and landscapes) or pad (wasting compute), we use aspect-ratio bucketing: a small set of allowed (w, h) shapes, with each image snapped to the nearest one and only same-shape images batched together.

We bucket in two steps. First by resolution tier (pixel count): a 512px and a 1024px tier for most of the corpus, plus 2048px and 4096px tiers for high-resolution data. An image goes into the largest tier it can reach without upscaling by more than 4/3 (~33%), so each tier's floor is (size × 3/4)² (≈384² for the 512 tier, 768² for 1024); anything below the smallest floor is dropped. Then by aspect ratio within the tier: we enumerate the patch-aligned (w, h) shapes (both divisible by 16, AR in [0.5, 2.0]) that keep a roughly constant ~256-patch token budget, giving 13 buckets per tier, from 0.5 (tall) through 1.0 (square) to 2.0 (wide). At 512px that's 352×704 … 512×512 … 704×352; at 1024px the same 13 ratios scaled up. Constant patch count keeps per-image compute flat across shapes.

Each image is then resized to its bucket with a Lanczos filter and encoded as JPEG at quality 92, and Mosaic Data Shards are written into a tree keyed by resolution and aspect ratio so the trainer can stream buckets separately:

The exploration in Section 2 relied on whatever captions a dataset shipped with. Once our own detailed captions were in place, the same full-text search became far more powerful, and a few passes over the captions turned up things the sparser original metadata had hidden: more text-heavy images (screenshots, slides, documents, infographics) than we had estimated, and some NSFW content that had slipped through.

To turn those approximate searches into a filter, we ran a quick classification pass with Qwen3-8B in text-only mode: it reads each caption (never the image) and labels the sample visual, text, or nsfw. The whole heuristic is essentially one question, "Would you look at this image, or read it?" Classifying from the caption rather than the pixels is cheap (around 200 captions/s per GPU) and reuses work we had already done. A pixel-level image classifier would likely be more accurate, but this was good enough to remove the obvious cases at moderate cost and without having to annotate data and train a custom classifier.

Rather than rewrite the whole corpus to drop these samples, we added a skip-list feature to the MDS data loader: a small sidecar file per shard lists the sample indices to skip, and the loader unions them and skips those samples at training time. Nothing is deleted or rewritten. This turned out to be a flexible mechanism well beyond this one filter. We can exclude any set of examples identified after the fact, whether a newly discovered quality issue, a blacklist, or, importantly, data from users who later opt out of having their content used for training, simply by extending the skip list before the next run. It is also convenient for ablations: to measure a filter's effect, train once with the skip list and once without, off the same dataset, instead of storing two copies. The one limit is scale. Skip lists add a little per-sample work at load time, so once the skipped fraction grows large (we would estimate somewhere around 10%, though we have not measured the crossover), it becomes worth rewriting the MDS dataset without the skipped samples rather than carrying an ever-growing skip list.

The same explorer surfaced a fair number of duplicates: large image collections tend to accumulate exact and near-duplicate copies, which waste training compute and skew the distribution. We mainly targeted near-duplicates and exact copies, so we added a quick deduplication pass using perceptual hashes. If the goal is to identify duplicate concepts and balance them in a dataset, deduplication based on clusters of image embeddings is a more suitable approach.

We could have done an exact dedup on a byte hash like SHA-256, but a perceptual hash already subsumes that (it matches byte-identical images too) while also catching re-encoded or resized copies, so we used only the perceptual hash. It is a standard DCT-based perceptual hash (downscale to a small grayscale thumbnail, 2D DCT, threshold the low-frequency coefficients into a compact fingerprint), implemented in a few lines on top of OpenCV and SciPy. We consider two hashes a match if their Hamming distance is zero, so we only remove near-pixel-identical copies. Genuinely different shots of the same subject have different fingerprints (and different captions) and are kept on purpose.

Once every image has a perceptual hash (fingerprint), the dedup itself is just a hash-map lookup: scanning each aspect-ratio bucket across resolutions, we keep one entry per fingerprint, so any image whose fingerprint we have already seen is a duplicate of the one we kept, and when a cluster spans resolutions we keep the highest-resolution copy. The duplicates are written out as a per-shard skip list that the loader unions and skips at load time, so nothing is deleted and the dataset is never rewritten.

Across the corpus, deduplication removed on the order of a few percent of images, the caption-based text filter a few percent more, and the NSFW pass a small fraction of a percent.

The dataset described here is the pre-training corpus, where breadth and scale matter most. For supervised fine-tuning and preference alignment the trade flips entirely: quality matters far more than quantity, and the problem becomes finding and curating small, high-signal subsets out of this large corpus. To do that we have been building more powerful curation tooling, including a richer explorer that tags images with structured attributes predicted by a VLM so we can assemble highly targeted subsets for fine-tuning. We plan to dig into topics like fine-tuning and preference alignment as well as the data tooling we use for these in a future post.

Build something with PRX, or find a bug in our pipeline? PRX is Apache 2.0 and the model code lives at github.com/Photoroom/PRX. We integrated PRX into the diffusers library and there is a Hugging Face Space to try out our latest version PRX Pixel.

Come talk diffusion models and data with us on Discord.

Public test Space for pixel-space PRX t2i

Thanks so much, Photoroom team, for sharing your experiences from PRX so far!! Learned a lot.

Public test Space for pixel-space PRX t2i

#10003. Blue Origin unveils more thrust, less haste as New Glenn slips to 2027

Staff memo pushes return to flight into January, overshadowing third-stage and engine announcements

New Glenn's return to flight has slipped to January 2027, according to the internal memo, viewed by The Register, from Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp, overshadowing the company's announcements of a new third stage and booster engine.

Blue Origin has been rebuilding after its New Glenn rocket exploded during a ground test in May, extensively damaging the launchpad.

A month later, the company's CEO, Dave Limp, said that Blue Origin "still plan[s] to fly again this year," which raised a few eyebrows in the space and rocket community. The detonation had pretty much destroyed the facility, and getting back into the launch business so quickly seemed optimistic.

That timetable has now slipped. In the memo, Limp praised the team's efforts but said: "We're proactively updating our anticipated launch date to January 2027."

A small slip given the damage, but one that leaves less breathing room before NASA's planned Artemis III demonstration mission, involving lunar technologies from Blue Origin and SpaceX, next year.

The delay emerged as the Bezos-backed company unveiled GS3, a third stage for New Glenn, designed for missions including direct injection into geostationary orbit and Earth-escape trajectories. The company said: "GS3 is already under contract for a cislunar mission with a government customer scheduled to launch in 2028."

Blue Origin says the stage is not required for its lunar lander architecture, although it could support sustained operations around the Moon.

The company also unveiled Northstar, a booster engine it says has half the parts and 30 percent less mass than its BE-4, while increasing thrust from 640,000 to 715,000 pounds-force.

The memo said the team had "found and fixed the issue that caused the anomaly," without elaborating. Limp said in August that the problem "originated at the main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines" and that existing engines would need retrofitting, but did not explain how the valve failed or what changes were required.The memo added that the company would "continue sharing progress updates on Voyager ." ®

#10002. 9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Practical guidance on safer search, stronger login security, better executive protection, and other habits can reduce enterprise risk.

9 Cybersecurity Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Threats

Cybersecurity Awareness Month tends to bring no shortage of advice, but the most useful guidance for business readers is the kind that maps to the way attacks actually happen now: through everyday habits, trusted workflows, and small moments of inattention. Risks show up when employees trust a search result, follow a fake CAPTCHA prompt, scan a login QR code, click a social ad, reuse a weak recovery method, or assume that an artificial intelligence (AI) model, executive device, or home network is secure by default. This article, compiled by the Dark Reading staff, and the accompanying videos bring those risks together in one place and focus on the practical behaviors and controls that can reduce them.

In October, a Dark Reading poll asked site visitors, "What's your biggest Cybersecurity Awareness Month challenge?" Readers identified phishing and social engineering as the top risk (39.1% of respondents), but that was neck-and-neck with shadow AI and risky data sharing (38.2%). A distant third was training fatigue and weak follow-through, identified as the top problem by 13.5% of respondents, and third-party and contractor access, with 9.2% of the vote.

Reader responses when asked, "What's your biggest Cybersecurity Awareness Month challenge?" Source: Dark Reading

The following nine tips can move the dial on that enterprise risk in very real ways. A common thread for all of these is the fact that attackers win by abusing convenience, familiarity, and human trust, whether the issue is SEO poisoning, ClickFix, session hijacking, dark patterns, or dodgy ads on Facebook. That's why awareness training still matters. It shouldn't be a once-a-year affair either, but rather an everyday focus on a set of specific, repeatable habits backed by stronger enterprise safeguards.

For security leaders, Cybersecurity Awareness Month gives them the chance to do more than remind users to "be careful." It is an opportunity to push for better defaults: phishing-resistant multifactor authentication (MFA), tighter privilege controls, better reporting paths, safer browsing habits, stronger executive protection, and more realistic guidance for work that happens outside the office. The goal is to make the safe action the default action and to help employees recognize the red flags before a routine click becomes a business problem.

Embrace cybersecurity awareness in October and beyond with Dark Reading's curated hub for security leaders — featuring expert news, analysis, and insights for hardening enterprise defenses in areas like identity security, AI risk, social engineering, supply chain, and more.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Becky Bracken, Media & Projects Director at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

As enterprises look to embrace agentic AI, they're sorting through frontier models, open-weight alternatives, and overseas offerings. Much of the focus is on evaluating the safeguards that, say, Claude might have vs. an open-weight alternative, like Meta's Llama series. But for business leaders, the key question is not which model is inherently safe; it's whether your organization has put adequate controls around it. That means treating AI just like any other high-impact enterprise system that can be misconfigured, manipulated, abused, or compromised.

Every model type comes with trade-offs. Frontier models may offer stronger vendor tooling, safety features, and governance support, but they can also introduce concentration and third-party risk. Open-weight models can give enterprises more transparency and control, but that control comes with more responsibility for hardening, patching, monitoring, and misuse prevention. Either way, the burden is on the enterprise.

For Cybersecurity Awareness Month, the practical takeaway is to assume compromise and build from there. Security teams should treat model weights, code, training data, prompts, plug-ins, APIs, and downstream applications as one attack surface. Limit what models can access. Restrict permissions. Segment AI workloads from critical systems. Log activity aggressively. Test for prompt injection, data leakage, and identity abuse. And keep humans in the loop for consequential actions, especially when money, customer data, or operational decisions are involved.

This is a golden opportunity for cybersecurity teams to become business enablers in the best sense of the term. AI will move fast, vendors will keep promising better safeguards, and the market will keep generating noise. But the durable security advantage will come from steady internal discipline. AI models can help the business, but they cannot be trusted to protect the business.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Alex Culafi, Senior News Writer at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

ClickFix is a simple but effective attack because it exploits something security teams deal with every day: people trying to solve a problem quickly. The user lands on a compromised or malicious Web site, a phishing page, or a fake browser-based meeting screen and sees what looks like a normal verification or troubleshooting prompt.

But instead of asking them to check a box, the page tells them to open a system tool — often with Windows + R — and paste in a command that the site has already copied to their clipboard. Once they do, they can trigger the compromise themselves. Security researchers note that this technique has risen sharply and often relies on fake CAPTCHA or error messages that make the request seem routine.

No legitimate CAPTCHA, website, or meeting platform should ever ask a user to open Run, PowerShell, Terminal, or Command Prompt and paste in a script. A request like that should be treated as an immediate red flag. The attack works precisely because it looks like a harmless fix and can sidestep some browser-based protections by pushing the user to execute the command themselves.

Organizations should build this into awareness training now. Tell employees to stop immediately if a website asks them to copy and paste commands, press unusual key combinations, or "fix" an issue through a local system tool. Reinforce a simple rule: If a prompt moves from the browser into the operating system, assume it's suspicious until IT says otherwise. Also, make it easy to report these incidents fast because early notification can help security teams contain the damage and identify affected users quickly. Restricting access to system tools where appropriate can add another layer of defense.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Rob Wright, Senior News Director at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

For Cybersecurity Awareness Month, here's a useful reminder for business leaders and employees alike: Treat social media ads as untrusted content. According to Gen Digital research, nearly one in three (31%) ads on Instagram and Facebook lead to scams, phishing pages, or malware.

And according to Reuters, Meta is charging higher premiums for advertisers that are considered risky. So not only have these platforms turned into a virtual minefield of scams, but Meta has a financial incentive to keep these ads online.

That matters because malicious ads often don't look malicious. They may mimic legitimate brands, use convincing creative, and point to spoofed URLs that appear credible at first glance. Even security-aware users can get caught. The real danger is that these ads exploit trust, urgency, and familiarity — exactly the tactics that work on busy professionals who are clicking quickly on personal devices outside the protections of corporate security tools.

The best defensive habit is simple: Do not click directly from social ads to make purchases, log in, or share payment information. If an offer looks legitimate, navigate to the brand's site manually, use a bookmarked link, or search for the company independently. Before entering credentials or card details, verify the domain carefully. Organizations should reinforce this behavior in security awareness training, especially for executives and remote workers who often blend personal and professional device use.

Caution remains the first line of defense. Encourage employees to use payment cards with fraud alerts, enable MFA on shopping and social accounts, and maintain healthy skepticism toward "limited-time" deals delivered through ad feeds.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Arielle Waldman, Features Writer at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

Ransomware has moved beyond encrypting systems and stealing data. Increasingly, attackers are pressuring organizations by targeting the people around their leaders: spouses, children, relatives, and close friends.

The "Semperis 2026 Ransomware Risk Report" found that 37% of attacks involved threats against employees' friends or family members. In other words, if attackers can't break your defenses fast enough, they may try to break your people instead. AI is accelerating this shift by making reconnaissance faster and cheaper, and threat actors can mine social media, public records, leaked data, and digital breadcrumbs to map relationships, impersonate trusted contacts, and build highly convincing social engineering campaigns.

For Cybersecurity Awareness Month, organizations should expand executive protection beyond the corporate perimeter. Start with digital footprint reduction: Encourage executives and family members to limit public exposure, remove unnecessary personal details from social profiles, and use aliases or less identifiable display names where practical. Establish family verification procedures, including safe words or challenge-response phrases, but rotate them regularly because any phrase used in a compromised channel should be treated as burned.

Most importantly, extend basic cyber hygiene to the household. Require strong unique passwords, enforce MFA on personal and shared accounts, secure home networks and connected devices, and train family members to recognize urgency-based scams, impersonation attempts, and suspicious content. A child's gaming console, a spouse's reused password, or a relative's overshared profile can become the opening attackers need.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Fahmida Rashid, Editor-in-Chief at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

Security awareness works better when it feels practical and relevant, not like a mandatory lecture. But one lesson is worth stating plainly: Some employees need more protection simply because they hold more power, more access, and more sensitive information. That starts with the C-suite, but it also applies to executive assistants, finance leaders, admins, and anyone else with privileged access.

Executives are high-value targets because they combine authority, visibility, and convenience-driven work habits. They approve payments, access sensitive strategy, and often log in from airports, hotels, and personal devices. That makes them especially attractive for phishing, impersonation, business email compromise, deepfake scams, and data theft. The right response is not to make life easier for them. It's to add smart friction in the places that matter most.

A strong executive protection program should include:

Phishing-resistant MFA, ideally hardware-based rather than SMS codes

Just-in-time privileged access instead of standing elevated permissions

Dedicated, locked-down devices for sensitive work

Stronger email and DLP controls to catch unusual forwarding, sharing, or exfiltration patterns

Focused coaching for executives and their inner circle, including assistants and chiefs of staff

Guidance for family and home networks because executive risk doesn't stop at the office

Organizations can focus on "white-glove" security, which means tighter controls, better support, and faster escalation when something looks off. If a control feels mildly annoying, that may be a sign it is doing its job.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Arielle Waldman, Features Writer at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

These design tricks train people to click quickly, surrender data reflexively, and ignore warning signs. Over time, that weakens judgment. Employees who get used to manipulative prompts may be less likely to notice when a request is truly malicious — whether that's a fake consent banner, a spoofed login page, a bogus app permission screen, or a prompt asking for sensitive information. Dark patterns blur the line between annoying and dangerous.

Another good rule: If you didn't sign up for a tool, don't create an account just because an email nudges you to. Unapproved sign-ups can create shadow accounts that IT and security teams can't monitor or secure.

Finally, build a reporting culture around anything that feels off — surprise charges, mystery accounts, unusual permissions, or suspicious prompts. The more comfortable employees are raising small concerns, the easier it is to catch bigger issues before they spread.

Everyone knows password hygiene remains a challenge for most businesses, but risk in the login journey increasingly extends to the other seams around identity — the moments where users, devices, sessions, and recovery workflows intersect.

The threats include quishing, where a user scans a QR code from an email, Web page, or physical sign and lands on a convincing but malicious login screen. There's also push fatigue, where attackers bombard a user with approval requests until one gets accepted. And it includes session hijacking and token theft, where the attacker skips the password entirely and hops into an already authenticated session. Add SIM swapping to intercept SMS-based recovery, and the modern login chain starts to look brittle in several different places.

The long-term fix is to move toward phishing-resistant authentication, including FIDO2 security keys and passkeys, backed by enterprise controls that verify context, not just credentials. That requires checking device posture, monitoring session behavior, requiring managed devices for sensitive systems, and reauthenticating when risk changes. In short: Don't just trust the login — trust the device, the session, and the user behavior behind it.

However, if this kind of full passkey rollout is not on the docket yet, here are some practical steps organizations can take now to reduce login risk:

Turn on number matching for push-based MFA

Reduce or eliminate SMS-based authentication where possible

Shorten session lifetimes for high-risk apps

Require managed-device access for sensitive systems

Trigger reauthentication when device posture changes

Meanwhile, employee training should focus on a few clear habits: Don't scan login QR codes from unsolicited messages or unverified sources, for one, and never approve an unexpected SMS verification push.

To prevent session hijacking, log out of accounts when you finish using them, rather than just closing the browser tab. And avoid public Wi-Fi when you're doing something sensitive.

Finally, on the SIM-swapping front, switch from SMS MFA to Authenticator Apps that can't be intercepted via a phone network. You can also request that account changes require physical ID in-store or multilayered, out-of-band authentication before processing SIM changes.

Account takeover attacks are a bugbear that is unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but increasing friction and cost for attackers throughout the login process can truly help and, hopefully at the very least, get you out of the low-hanging-fruit category.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Rob Wright, Senior News Director at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

Fall youth sports season means many parent-professionals are working from the sidelines — at soccer fields, hockey rinks, football stadiums, and school gyms — often on whatever free Wi-Fi happens to be available. That may not sound as risky as logging on at a major airport or hotel, but it still creates an opportunity for mistakes that attackers, pranksters, or opportunistic snoops can exploit.

So, although sophisticated nation-state actors are probably not camping out at your local rink, there's still considerable risk if you connect to the wrong network. A hotspot with a name that closely resembles the venue's legitimate Wi-Fi can be enough to trick a busy parent checking email between periods or joining a meeting from the bleachers. Even a spoofed network set up as a joke can expose traffic, credentials, or session data if employees are careless.

Business readers that want to avoid their employer's penalty box should treat public connectivity anywhere as untrusted by default. Before joining a network, verify the exact Wi-Fi name with venue staff or posted signage. Disable auto-join so your device does not connect to similarly named networks without your knowledge. Use only approved secure remote access tools, keep endpoint protections enabled, and avoid handling sensitive work, such as admin access, financial approvals, or password resets, over public Wi-Fi unless it is absolutely necessary.

If you need connectivity, a personal hotspot is often the safer option — but only if it is configured properly. Use a strong password, change the default network name if it reveals your identity, and make sure the hotspot is not left open to nearby devices.

The broader lesson for Cybersecurity Awareness Month: Low-profile locations can still produce real security failures. The setting may feel routine, but the network risk is not.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Alex Culafi, Senior News Writer at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

SEO poisoning turns a routine Google search into an attack path. Threat actors either build lookalike websites or compromise legitimate ones, then manipulate content and code so those pages rank highly in search results. The idea is that a user searching for software, a login page, or a partner site might simply click the top result, which happens to be poisoned, and subsequently hand over credentials or download malware.

Guidance on spotting fake websites specifically warns that SEO poisoning can push malicious sites to the top of search results, and Trend Micro's 2026 research on more than 35,000 fake World Cup-related sites shows how easily attackers can industrialize fake-site campaigns around high-interest topics.

For business users, the safest habit is to stop trusting search rankings as a signal of legitimacy. Before clicking, inspect the URL for misspellings, extra words, odd country codes, or brand names that look slightly off. After clicking, be suspicious if the page immediately pushes a download, asks for credentials too early, triggers repeated redirects, throws pop-ups, or trips a browser warning. Those are strong signs that something is wrong.

Organizations should reinforce a few simple rules in awareness training:

Use bookmarks or manually typed URLs for key business apps, vendors, and partner portals.

Verify domains before downloading software or entering credentials.

Treat urgent install prompts and so-called ClickFix instructions as red flags.

Report suspicious search results, spoofed pages, and accidental downloads to IT immediately.

Isolate the device and change credentials quickly if a user may have interacted with a fake site.

The practical message for Cybersecurity Awareness Month: Search is a convenience layer, not a trust layer. Employees don't need to become threat hunters, but they do need to slow down long enough to verify where a search result is actually taking them. That pause can prevent a compromise.

#10001. LeRobot v0.6.0: Imagine, Evaluate, Improve

This new release is about closing the robot learning loop: policies that imagine the future before acting, reward models that tell you when your robot succeeds, a deployment CLI that turns failures into training data, and six new simulation benchmarks to measure it all. It also brings depth sensing, VLM-powered dataset annotation, custom video encoding, cloud training on HF Jobs, and a much leaner install.

LeRobot v0.6.0 introduces world model policies (VLA-JEPA, FastWAM, LingBot-VA) that learn to imagine the future, a wave of new VLAs (GR00T N1.7, MolmoAct2, EO-1, EVO1, Multitask DiT), and a new reward models API (Robometer, TOPReward). It ships six new simulation benchmarks unified under lerobot-eval, the lerobot-rollout CLI with DAgger-style human-in-the-loop corrections, FSDP training, and cloud training on HF Jobs. Datasets get depth support, an automatic language annotation pipeline, custom video encoding, and up to 2x faster data loading, all on top of a leaner installation.

The robotics world is asking a big question: do world models actually help robot policies? v0.6.0 brings three policies to LeRobot to help answer that question. Each one learns to imagine the future as part of its training, and each takes a different path to keep that imagination affordable.

VLA-JEPA teaches a compact VLA (built on Qwen3-VL-2B) to predict the future in latent space while it learns to act: during training, a JEPA world model has to anticipate upcoming frames from the model's own actions. The trick is that the world model then disappears at inference, so you get world-model supervision at zero extra inference cost. Three ready-to-use checkpoints are on the Hub, including a DROID-pretrained base for fine-tuning:

Check out the VLA-JEPA documentation and the paper to learn more.

LingBot-VA goes one step further: an autoregressive video-action model that predicts future video and actions together, chunk by chunk, and feeds real observations back in to keep its imagination grounded. You can even save what the robot imagined (--policy.save_predicted_video=true) and compare it with what actually happened. Inference runs on a single 24–32 GB GPU. Check out the documentation and the paper for the technical details.

FastWAM asks the question in its paper title: do world action models need test-time future imagination? It pairs a ~5B video-generation expert with a compact action expert in a single network, so the model literally learns to dream its own rollouts. At inference it skips the dreaming entirely and directly denoises action chunks. Fine-tune it from lerobot/fastwam_base, and read more in the documentation.

We upgraded our NVIDIA GR00T integration to GR00T N1.7, the newest open generation of NVIDIA's cross-embodiment foundation model. N1.7 swaps the previous VLM for Cosmos-Reason2-2B (built on Qwen3-VL) feeding a flow-matching action head, and our integration is parity-tested against NVIDIA's original Isaac-GR00T implementation: same inputs, same outputs. Flash-attention is now optional, so pip install 'lerobot[groot]' just works, and you can load NVIDIA's published checkpoints directly.

GR00T N1.7 replaces N1.5 in LeRobot. If you need N1.5, pin lerobot==0.5.1.

MolmoAct2, the Allen Institute for AI's vision-language-action model, is now ported into LeRobot with the full lifecycle covered: fine-tuning (full or LoRA), evaluation, and real-robot deployment. Ready-made checkpoints with calibration correction baked in mean you can run it zero-shot on an SO-100/101:

Inference fits in ~12 GB at bf16, and LoRA fine-tuning fits on a single 24 GB GPU. See the MolmoAct2 documentation for the full deployment guide.

EO-1, a VLA pretrained upstream on interleaved vision-text-action data, joins LeRobot: a Qwen2.5-VL-3B backbone with a flow-matching action head, contributed by one of the paper's own authors. Train it with the standard lerobot-train workflow using --policy.type=eo1. Details in the documentation and the paper.

The Multitask Diffusion Transformer policy brings the TRI Large Behavior Models recipe to LeRobot: a ~450M-parameter diffusion transformer conditioned on CLIP vision and language embeddings, so one model learns many tasks selected via natural language. It supports both diffusion and flow-matching objectives, and it is small enough to train yourself. See the documentation.

VLAs don't have to be huge. EVO1 packs its policy into 0.77B parameters, an InternVL3-1B backbone with a flow-matching action head, small enough to fine-tune and run in real time on modest GPUs. It ships with two-stage fine-tuning and Real-Time Chunking support out of the box. See the EVO1 documentation and the paper.

Success detection and progress estimation are missing pieces in the robot learning loop, and v0.6.0 gives them a home. LeRobot now has a unified reward models API (lerobot.rewards), mirroring the policies API, with four reward models behind one interface - the HIL-SERL reward classifier, SARM, and two new additions:

Robometer is a pretrained, general-purpose reward model: point lerobot/Robometer-4B at any LeRobot dataset and it scores task progress and success from raw video plus a language instruction, with no task-specific training required. It is built on Qwen3-VL-4B and trained via trajectory comparisons over a dataset of more than one million robot trajectories (RSS 2026 paper).

TOPReward goes fully zero-shot: no reward weights at all. It wraps an off-the-shelf VLM (Qwen3-VL) and reads the log-probability of the token "True" given the trajectory video and the task instruction. Any capable VLM becomes a reward function.

Both ship with labeling scripts that write per-frame progress curves into your dataset, ready for reward-aware behavior cloning (RA-BC), dataset quality inspection, and progress-overlay videos. Check the Robometer and TOPReward docs.

Recording is no longer stuck with one hard-coded codec. The new --dataset.rgb_encoder.* options expose the full encoding surface (codec, quality, pixel format, GOP, presets), and vcodec=auto probes for hardware encoders like NVENC, VideoToolbox, VAAPI, and QSV before falling back to the default software AV1 encoder. For existing datasets, one command re-encodes everything:

Full details in the video encoding documentation.

Plug in an Intel RealSense, set use_depth: true, and LeRobot records depth maps end to end: captured in millimeters, compressed as compact 12-bit depth video streams alongside your RGB cameras, and decoded back to physical units at training time. Depth renders live during recording and in lerobot-dataset-viz, and it works across SO-100/101, Koch, OpenArm, reBot, Unitree G1 and more.

Your dataset stops being one task string per episode. LeRobot datasets now natively store rich language annotations (timestamped subtasks, plans, memory, corrections, speech, and per-camera VQA pairs), and the new lerobot-annotate CLI fills them in automatically using a VLM that watches your episodes:

A YAML recipe layer then renders these annotations into chat-style training messages at sample time: exactly the data tomorrow's long-horizon, talking robot policies will train on. Scale it up with HF Jobs, and read the annotation pipeline docs to learn more.

Training on video datasets is now up to ~2x faster out of the box: multi-camera frames decode in parallel, dataloader workers ship compact uint8 frames (4x less memory between processes), and persistent workers keep decoder caches alive across epochs. Loading a subset of a large dataset (episodes=[...]) went from minutes to milliseconds (275 s down to 0.06 s in our benchmark). Sampling is also deterministic and resumable now, so interrupted trainings restart sample-exact.

v0.5.0 planted the flag on LeRobot as an evaluation hub for VLAs; v0.6.0 makes it the real deal with six new simulation benchmarks, all runnable through the same lerobot-eval CLI, each with a docs page, a Docker image, and a SmolVLA baseline checkpoint smoke-tested in CI:

Simulator backends require specific system dependencies with their own install steps; each docs page has the exact recipe, and every benchmark ships a ready-made Docker image if you'd rather skip the setup.

Together with LIBERO, Meta-World, and NVIDIA IsaacLab-Arena, that makes nine benchmark families under one roof, and a new Adding a New Benchmark guide documents exactly how to plug in yours. Evaluation also got faster: parallel eval now defaults to async vectorized environments, benchmarked at up to 2x faster.

Deploying a policy used to be a hack on top of lerobot-record. The new lerobot-rollout CLI makes deployment its own workflow, with pluggable strategies and inference backends (including Real-Time Chunking for slow compatible VLAs). The base strategy just runs the policy. sentry records continuously, rotating episodes and uploading to the Hub as it goes. highlight keeps a ring buffer and saves the last N seconds when you hit a key, so an interesting moment is never lost. episodic mirrors the classic episode/reset recording workflow. And dagger turns deployment into data collection.

With the DAgger strategy, you watch your policy run, hit a key (or a USB foot pedal) the moment it goes wrong, take over with your leader arm to record the correction, and hand control back. Actuated leaders are driven to the follower's pose before you take over, so the handover is jerk-free. Every correction frame is tagged with an intervention flag, and the resulting dataset is ready for the next fine-tune:

Deploy, collect corrections, fine-tune, repeat: the robot learning flywheel is now a CLI flag. Read the deployment docs.

Robot foundation models are outgrowing single GPUs. LeRobot training now supports FSDP (fully sharded data parallel) through Accelerate: parameters, gradients, and optimizer state are sharded across GPUs, and checkpoints are gathered back into a plain single-file model.safetensors that loads like any other policy. You can even resume an FSDP run on a different number of GPUs. See the multi-GPU training docs.

No GPU? No problem. The exact same lerobot-train command now runs in the cloud by adding one flag:

LeRobot pushes your local dataset to a private Hub repo if needed, submits the job, streams logs to your terminal, and pushes the trained policy to the Hub at the end. Pick anything from a T4 to 8x H200 with --job.target (compute is billed pay-as-you-go). Check out the documentation

Check the release notes for the full list and migration pointers for the breaking changes.

Beyond these headline features, v0.6.0 includes hundreds of bug fixes, documentation improvements, and quality-of-life upgrades across the codebase, from smarter defaults to more reliable CI.

We want to extend a huge thank you to everyone in the community. This release includes work from academia, industry and hobbyists teams who chose LeRobot as the home for their models and benchmarks. Every PR and bug report pushes open-source robotics forward.

Stay tuned for more to come 🤗 Get started here! – The LeRobot team ❤️

#10000. Crowd fave Linux Mint update approaches, fresh from autumn release of Cinnamon desktop

Mint 27 to land before Christmas, with stable Wayland display upgrades, as punters try out Cinnamon 6.8

Linux Mint 27 is expected next month, and it's starting to take shape. Its flagship desktop, Cinnamon 2.8, is already available.

The team behind the popular, beginner-friendly Linux just released Cinnamon 2.8, which will be the default desktop in Mint 27. Since 2014, Linux Mint versions have been based on the LTS releases of Ubuntu. Since a new LTS, Ubuntu 26.04 "Resolute Raccoon" arrived in late April, that means that a corresponding version of Mint is in development.

The Mint project blog post last month revealed the codename: "Adrien." This is the first male codename since Mint 1.0 "Ada" in 2006, based on the first ever Ubuntu LTS release, 6.06 "Dapper Drake", but the project has run through the whole alphabet since then (except for the letter “Y”.) That blog also revealed it will have a new alarm clock app, but the subsequent Mint Blog post imparted more information.

The Nemo file manager will gain a preview pane, there will be a new and much more capable system resource-monitor program called "Superlight", a new simple manager for compressed archive files (Zip and so on) called "Unfold," and a new, theme-able terminal emulator called "Velocitty." Mint also has a new Community Website, which uses GitHub to manage logins and eliminates the old website's dependency on PHP.

Probably the most significant new feature, though, is that Mint 27 will restore system hibernation. Ubuntu supported hibernation in its early releases, but it has been disabled as standard since 12.04 "Precise Pangolin." Enabling it again is regularly discussed, for instance back in 2020. As we discussed in some detail a year ago, it's a complicated subject and there's a lot that can go wrong.

It seems that Mint's Clément Lefebvre feels he can sort this, and we hope it works out. Support is included in the new version of Cinnamon, among a host of other changes. Its Wayland support is no longer experimental, although the X11 session is still there so users won't be forced to use the new system. The Network Manager applet has better, simpler VPN support and Wi-Fi encryption handling. There are multiple improvements across the desktop: better handling of sound devices, keyboard input layouts, touchpads and gesture support, HiDPI display handling, and better search in the Settings app. The window list control has been upgraded, more things happen in the background for faster desktop starts, and it has better handling and storage of authentication and credentials, including the same Rust-based "oo7" secret store we mentioned in Fedora 45. Screensaver handling is also mentioned – this is particularly problematic under Wayland, as XScreensaver maintainer Jamie Zawinski has covered with some feeling. The Mint blog mentioned this at the start of 2026, when Lefebvre announced the new, slower, annual release schedule.

Cinnamon is not the only desktop environment that has moved to embrace Wayland while also maintaining its support for X.org. Almost exactly two years ago, we reported that the LXQt 2.1 included preliminary Wayland support. That project is very much still in active development, led by Jen-Lee "PCMan" Hong, and version 2.5.0 just appeared, almost simultaneously with Cinnamon 2.8.

Before LXQt, "PCMan" developed the LXDE desktop – which is still around. There's an LXDE spin of Fedora 45, the Raspberry Pi OS uses some of its components, and last year when Debian 13 was released we also noted that its terminal emulator, LXTerminal, had just been updated. This release of LXQt removes its last dependency on an LXDE component – until now, it still used the old menu-cache.

LXQt 2.5 is based on Qt 6.10, and it draws upon some of the components of KDE Plasma. One of these is libkscreen, which manages screens for Plasma. Version 6.8 of this drops X11 support – as does Plasma 6.8 itself – and that broke LXQt's Monitor Settings applet. The team are looking for a workaround and plan to fix this in a minor point release. Aside from this, the desktop's taskbar-style panel has improved sizing support, icon handling, and auto-hide, but most of the improvements in this release are in around its QTerminal terminal emulator.

New LXQt versions usually appear twice a year, around April and November, so this version will likely be in Lubuntu 27.04 in about five months – and available in many other distributions, too. ®

#9998. Germany Busts 'Crime-as-a-Service' Investment Fraud Outfit

Authorities seized more than 100 servers and arrested seven as part of a crackdown on a fraud network spanning more than 50 countries.

You see an online advertisement promising quick returns from trading cryptocurrency, foreign currencies, and stocks. You give the "investment firm" your information, and an operator calls you and convinces you to transfer a small amount of money into a platform. You make early profits quickly, so you deposit increasingly large sums of money. But when you attempt to withdraw your earnings, the operator stalls for a while until finally cutting off contact.

This pattern is familiar to victims of investment fraud, a multinational criminal industry that relies on social engineering to convince would-be investors that they're about to make substantial gains before pulling the rug out from under them.

Europol today shared news of the disruption of one such operation, an investment fraud scheme with potential victims across more than 50 countries and a company allegedly supplying fraudulent trading platforms and leads to criminal groups. According to a press release, Europol and Eurojust supported an international operation involving authorities in Albania, Cyprus, Finland, Germany, Israel, Kosovo, and North Macedonia.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

The German Itzehoe Public Prosecutor's Office led the operation, targeting a company suspected of supplying phony trading websites and multiple call centers to criminal groups; investigators estimate losses to exceed 4 million euros.

International authorities searched 17 locations, including a call center in Kosovo, leading to the seizure of 100 servers and the arrests of seven suspects.

The law enforcement action reflects a multiyear investigation that began in 2022, according to Europol, when a German couple reported they could not withdraw money invested through an online trading platform. This led to two previous "action days" by authorities, one in 2022 (involving two arrests and the seizure of evidence) and another in 2025 (involving more arrests and seizures of money and evidence).

"Analysis of the material recovered exposed the suspected infrastructure provider and its links to call centre operators, paving the way for the latest operation," the press release read.

A Eurojust press release provided further detail regarding the extent of the operation. The analysis of evidence seized during the second action day exposed a company based in Cyprus and Israel allegedly offering "crime-as-a-service," supplying criminal groups with fraudulent websites that funnel targets into the central investment scam.

The data of potential victims visiting these websites and expressing interest would be sold as leads to call centers, which contacted the victims to persuade them to invest their money, leading to repeated demands for additional investments. Authorities identified suspected call center-operating clients of this company in Albania, Kosovo, and North Macedonia.

Related:UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk

The fraud operation guaranteed significant returns for trades in cryptocurrencies, foreign currencies, or stocks, according to Europol. But authorities found that the seemingly legitimate platforms were run by "brokers" that used phony profits and social engineering tactics to convince victims to keep investing. Additionally, investigators also found the operators used affiliate marketing services and deceptive advertisements to lure in potential victims.

Austin Anderson, director of threat intel at cybercrime disruption firm Netcraft, tells Dark Reading that operations like these that target upstream providers can help disrupt investment fraud operations at scale.

"Fraudsters have increasingly specialized in one piece of an attack's supply chain, as seen in this scheme where websites collected personal data that was sold to call centers to ultimately coerce funds from victims," he says. "While this can breed sophistication in each actor's niche, it also introduces fragility when a large dependency like the call center is disrupted. Ultimately, without arrests that remove fraudsters from the market, these operations only temporarily disrupt operations while actors rebuild their infrastructure."

Related:US Government Email Systems Open to Abuse Thanks to Typos

#9997. Nspawn 3.0: A Docker-compatible Engine API for systemd-nspawn containers

Everything you need to know about systemd-nspawn.

2.0.0 gave the machines that mount docker’s socket a read-only Docker API, enough for Traefik or Dozzle to find them. 3.0.0 serves the API with its changes, on the host too. In between:

The host’s socket is /run/nspawn/api.sock, opened by nspawn-api.socket. Its main purpose is compatibility: tools that manage containers through the Docker API, like GitLab Runner’s docker executor, can use nspawn’s machines instead. nspawn is still the command line for managing them, but the docker command works against the socket too.

The packages ship the socket turned off. Once it listens, nspawn-api.service starts on the first connection:

With DOCKER_HOST pointing at it, the docker command talks to nspawn:

The API server is a client of the bus service, as the command line is. Everything it does is a method of org.nspawn, under the same polkit actions: reads and waits need org.nspawn.inspect, logs and changes need org.nspawn.manage. Every user can connect, but polkit is never asked to prompt, since nothing on a socket can answer an authentication agent. Root can do everything, and any other user needs a polkit rule, like nspawn-wheel.rules, which the packages ship as an example. As with the docker group, a user with org.nspawn.manage is root on the host: a machine runs commands as root and can mount any host path.

What one socket’s clients hold at once (connections, log and event streams, waits, attaches, execs) is bounded, and a user other than root gets a share of each, so no user can keep the others or root out.

Clients that only look at /run/docker.sock find it with a drop-in, on a host where nothing else has that path:

It answers in the shapes of API 1.51, and of the versions down to 1.24 that clients ask for.

GitLab Runner’s docker executor runs its jobs on nspawn’s machines through the API. Its host setting points at the socket:

A variable’s value can now hold line breaks (-e, compose’s environment, the API’s Env). GitLab’s CI_COMMIT_MESSAGE for a commit with a body is one.

A machine’s API socket takes changes. In 2.0.0 the socket inside a machine was read-only. Now a machine that mounts /var/run/docker.sock, /run/docker.sock or /run/nspawn/api.sock read-write can create, start, exec in and remove containers, pull and remove images, and create volumes and networks. With :ro the socket reads, follows logs and kills, and refuses everything else with 403. Only root inside the machine can connect, and it sees every machine and their -e variables (--secret values never show). A proxy or a dashboard that only reads should mount it :ro, the Traefik example in the 2.0 post included: /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro.

The requirements are the same as for 2.0.0. Packages for Fedora, Debian/Ubuntu and Arch are attached to the release, and apt.nspawn.org and rpm.nspawn.org have the first two. If a client of the Docker API fails against nspawn where it works with docker, open an issue with what it sent.

#9996. Run AI workloads on any cloud, store on Hugging Face: zero-egress storage with SkyPilot

For most teams, models and datasets live in a bucket in one region of one cloud. The GPUs you can get, whether for development, training, or serving, increasingly sit on a different cloud than your data. The moment those two come apart, you pay a cross-cloud transfer tax just to read your own data onto your own GPUs.

Together with Hugging Face, we've joined the two halves: your models and datasets stay on the Hub, and SkyPilot runs the compute (dev, training, or serving) on whatever cluster has the GPUs. Mount a Hugging Face Bucket or any Hub repo into a SkyPilot job with one hf:// URL and the HF_TOKEN you already have, then launch it wherever capacity is. Hugging Face charges no egress, so reading your data onto those GPUs costs nothing, on any cloud.

SkyPilot tasks already read and write cloud object stores (S3, GCS, Azure, R2, and many more) by mounting them at a local path. Hugging Face Storage now joins that list as store: hf, reached through the hf:// scheme:

That one hf:// scheme covers the whole lifecycle: read the model and dataset from their repos, write checkpoints to a Bucket while you train, publish the finished model back to a repo, and pull it onto inference servers when you serve. Most teams already keep their models and datasets on the Hub, so there is no migration step and no new storage account to create.

MOUNT uses Hugging Face's hf-mount FUSE backend, so a bucket or repo shows up as a local path next to SkyPilot's other FUSE mounts (gcsfuse, blobfuse2, rclone, goofys). The fetching happens at the filesystem layer: when your code issues a read(), the driver pulls just those bytes from the Xet backend, so only the data you actually touch crosses the network, and hf-mount keeps an on-disk cache so repeat reads stay local. That on-disk cache is the behavior SkyPilot gives its other backends under MOUNT_CACHED, where a plain MOUNT instead streams every read from the bucket with nothing kept locally. For the hf store, MOUNT and MOUNT_CACHED behave the same, so either mode keeps the cache.

Because reads are lazy, a process can start working through a large file before the whole file has downloaded, instead of blocking on a full copy first. That keeps the GPU busy almost immediately, training on data as it streams in rather than sitting idle (and billing) while a dataset or checkpoint copies down. It pays off most on the first epoch, when nothing is cached yet. COPY takes the other route and downloads through huggingface_hub up front, with no special requirements.

Authentication is the token you already have. Set HF_TOKEN in your environment and hand it to a run with --secret HF_TOKEN; SkyPilot uses it for the mount on whatever cloud the job lands. One token works whether the job lands on AWS, GCP, Azure, Nebius, Lambda, or your own Kubernetes cluster, so there are no per-cloud bucket keys to juggle.

GPU capacity rarely comes from one place anymore. To get enough H100s and H200s, teams hold reserved and committed capacity across several vendors at once (a block on a hyperscaler, a cluster on a neocloud, maybe an on-prem rack) and run wherever they have allocation. SkyPilot is built for this: one job spec, scheduled across 20+ clouds, Kubernetes, and on-prem, landing on whichever reserved cluster is free.

Object storage has been the catch. Object stores are regional and per-cloud, so feeding a GPU or an inference server that sits in a different vendor's data center means either keeping a copy of your data in every vendor's bucket or paying to pull it across. Most clouds charge egress (around $0.09/GB out of AWS) the moment data leaves their network, and often between regions inside one cloud. Pulling a base model onto every inference node, or iterating a dataset for several epochs from a cluster on another cloud, adds a hefty bill on top of GPUs you have already reserved. Teams end up pinning each run to whichever vendor holds the data and leaving the rest of their capacity idle.

Hugging Face Storage takes that cost off the table where it bites: the read side. With no egress or CDN fees and storage at $12-18/TB/month (versus AWS S3 at roughly $23/TB plus egress), the same bucket is reachable from every one of those clusters, and reading from it is free no matter where the GPUs run. Writing back still costs your compute cloud's usual egress, the same as it would to any off-cloud store, but for most AI work the reads dominate: a dataset streamed over many epochs, or model weights pulled onto every new training or inference node. So you stop pinning each run to whichever vendor holds a copy of the data.

To collect some benchmark numbers, we ran a small fine-tune: Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B on the HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking dataset with TRL's SFTTrainer, mounting the model read-only from its Hub repo and writing every checkpoint to a Hugging Face Bucket. The same SkyPilot YAML ran on AWS, GCP, and Lambda, changing only --infra. SkyPilot placed each job wherever GPUs were free, and all three read and wrote the same bucket.

Per cloud, checkpoints wrote to the bucket at:

Hugging Face Buckets are built on Xet, which uses content-defined chunking to split files into ~64 KB chunks and store each unique chunk once. Because the boundaries follow the content, an edit changes only the chunks it touches and the rest are recognized as already stored. This pays off in a few places:

How much you save depends on how much your artifacts overlap, but the deduplication is automatic: you write a checkpoint as usual, and only the new chunks leave the machine.

Add an hf:// mount to any SkyPilot task and launch. MOUNT needs a base image with glibc 2.34+ and /dev/fuse.

The initial store: hf support started as a contribution from Nikhil Jha. The Hugging Face team carried it forward and upstreamed the hf-mount FUSE fixes that let it mount in unprivileged containers, the default on many Kubernetes clusters. The SkyPilot team wired it into the storage backend. The whole path is open source: SkyPilot, Hugging Face's hf-mount, and the huggingface_hub client.
